title: Music and movement intervention for brain-heart disease in children with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1): a convergent mixed-methods feasibility study protocol.
abstract: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a rare autosomal dominant inherited multi-systemic disease affecting neuromuscular, cognitive, and cardiac function. Congenital DM1 (CDM) is the most severe form of the disease and is associated with learning difficulties, autism-like traits, and cardiac conduction defects. There is no approved pharmacological therapy for CDM. While music interventions have been shown to positively impact children with similar brain and heart symptoms, like cerebral palsy and autism, this type of non-pharmacological intervention has not been tested in CDM. Therefore, this convergent mixed-methods study will assess the tolerability and feasibility of a 10-week music and movement intervention for children with CDM. Participants will be recruited from the pediatric neuromuscular clinic at the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO). In a dyad participation model, parents of participants will also engage to inform the overall feasibility. There will be two groups with 6-8 participants each. Group allocation will not be randomized but will be based on age and physical and mental ability. A baseline visit will be followed by a 10-week intervention phase with one music and movement intervention session per week. Sessions will include physical assessments and questionnaires. The primary outcome is the feasibility and tolerability of these music interventions. Secondary outcome measures include cognitive and physical assessments, as well as measures of quality of life, sleep quality, and biomarkers. This study will demonstrate the feasibility and tolerability of music and movement intervention for pediatric participants with CDM, while providing an indication of its impacts on brain and heart function for this multi-system disease. Results from this study will inform the implementation of a larger-scale trial as well as the development of other non-pharmacological feasibility studies in this population. Clinicaltrials.gov number: NCT06809049. Registered 30 Jan 2025. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06809049?id=NCT06809049&rank=1 .

title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
abstract: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission. This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants. All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome. Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

title: Effectiveness of virtual reality exposure therapy in improving body dissatisfaction and shape-related concerns in adolescent girls with anorexia nervosa: a controlled, randomized, superiority trial.
abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) involves qualitative and quantitative dietary restrictions, leading to significant weight loss and changes in body shape. Patients with AN are often more concerned about their body image than the general population is. Body dissatisfaction and shape-related concerns (BD-SRC), which are risk factors for relapse, are some of the most difficult AN symptoms to treat. This study aims to assess the effectiveness of Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET) in improving BD-SRC in adolescent girls with AN. This prospective, multicenter study will be a controlled, randomized, superiority trial. This study will be an open-ended trial. In total, 40 patients with AN will be randomly assigned to the "VRET" or the "body-first psychomotricity" group. Adolescent girls will be randomly divided into two groups: 20 each receiving VRET and 20 receiving treatment with body-first psychomotricity treatment. The primary objective will be rated 12 months after randomization using the Body Shape Questionnaire. The study hypothesizes that VRET is more effective than a body-first psychomotricity approach in improving BD-SRC and that this improvement is stable in the long term, even after treatment has stopped. If this hypothesis is confirmed, VRET could offer an interesting new therapeutic alternative to the traditional European approach of body-first psychomotricity for adolescent girls with AN. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials, NCT04107870, Registered on September 26, 2019. https://clinicaltrials.gov/show/NCT04107870 .

title: Structural features and disease-associated functions of ADGRV1: insights from signaling mechanisms.
abstract: Adhesion G protein-coupled receptor V1 (ADGRV1) is one of the largest and most modular receptors in the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor (aGPCR) family, integrating functions of cell adhesion, mechanosensing, and classical G protein signaling. Its structural domains, including calcium exchanger β (Calx-β) repeats, laminin G-like/ pentraxin (LamG/PTX) domain, epilepsy-associated (EPTP/EAR) repeats, GPCR-autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain/GPCR proteolytic site (GPS) module with tethered Stachel peptide, seven transmembrane (7TM) helices, and PDZ-binding motif (PBM), jointly shape its activation, intracellular transport, and effector coupling. Recent studies indicate that ADGRV1 exhibits context-dependent signaling, particularly through G protein coupling and ciliary localization, thereby influencing calcium homeostasis, autophagy, and developmental pathways. Genetic and functional evidence links ADGRV1 to Usher syndrome (USH) type II, epilepsy, and emerging associations with Alzheimer's disease (AD), and recurrent somatic alterations in diverse cancers. Variants in ADGRV1 modulate processes such as ankle-link complex (ALC) assembly, synaptic stability, amyloid and tau regulation, chemoresistance, and immune microenvironment remodeling. Despite this progress, many aspects of its signaling mechanisms, ligand interactions, and disease relevance remain poorly understood. Future work combining high-resolution structural studies, systematic mapping of signaling bias, and rigorous translational validation will be essential to clarify the multifaceted roles of ADGRV1 and to evaluate its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

title: Challenges in the diagnosis and management of coexisting drop-head syndrome and dysphagia: a case report and review of the literature.
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive diagnostic method for coexisting dropped head syndrome (DHS) and dysphagia, both associated with long-term complications of neck radiation. The symptoms reported are common after radiotherapy, but their co-occurrence, causal link, and the years since the initial treatments all contribute to the uniqueness of the case presented. A literature review on the topic is also included. A 54-year-old White male presented with progressive neck extensor weakness consistent with dropped head syndrome (DHS), associated with dysphagia and voice changes, occurring 17 years after radiotherapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma. A comprehensive clinical and instrumental evaluation, including a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS), electromyography (EMG), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), revealed mild-to-moderate dysphagia characterized by reduced swallowing efficiency, with residue in the valleculae and pyriform sinuses (> 50% occupancy) and a Penetration-Aspiration Scale score of 1 (no aspiration). The findings were consistent with postural and neuromuscular alterations involving the cervical region. Bolus clearance improved with manual head support. A structured 2-week rehabilitation program was associated with improved quality of life (as reported by improvement in the SWAL-QOL score) and stable nutritional status, though no objective physiological change was documented on the follow-up electromyographic exam. To our knowledge, this is the first work describing the importance of considering delayed-onset swallowing impairment associated with DHS in patients previously treated with radiotherapy for head-and-neck malignancies. The co-occurrence of DHS and dysphagia, both related to long-term complications of neck radiation, necessitates a comprehensive diagnostic approach that is currently lacking in the relevant literature. Swallowing assessments and screenings should be standard procedures in the long-term follow-up of tumors affecting the head-and-neck regions. The study underscores the importance of considering neuromuscular pathophysiological and mechanical mechanisms in post-radiotherapy dysphagia.

title: Astrocyte lipid metabolism in brain health and neurodegeneration: from regulatory hub to maladaptive stressor.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are increasingly recognized as multicellular pathologies in which astrocytes serve as active determinants of disease onset and progression. Central to the regulatory role of astrocytes is the precise and dynamic control of brain lipid homeostasis. This review discusses a framework positioning astrocytic lipid metabolism as a key axis of both brain metabolic health and neurodegenerative processes. Under physiological conditions, astrocytes operate as the primary lipid metabolic hub, coordinating de novo cholesterol synthesis, APOE-mediated lipid transport, and the uptake and degradation of fatty acids. However, upon aging, chronic stress, and proteinopathies, these homeostatic programs undergo profound adaptation and remodeling. We detail how the breakdown of astrocytic lipid handling-driven by genetic risk factors such as APOE4 and manifesting as cholesterol dyshomeostasis, aberrant lipid droplet accumulation, impaired lipid turnover, and pro-inflammatory lipid signaling-transforms astrocytes into maladaptive reactive states and contributes to neurodegeneration. This metabolic rewiring not only deprives vulnerable neurons of essential metabolic and structural support but actively amplifies neuroinflammation and neurotoxicity. Finally, we consider therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring functional lipid flux and mitigating lipid-driven pathogenic signaling. By examining neurodegeneration through the lens of astrocytic lipid metabolism, we highlight novel conceptual paradigms for understanding neurodegeneration and emerging translational opportunities for disease interventions.

title: Slow change blindness from serial dependence: slowly changing objects are perceived as biased toward the past.
abstract: Slow change blindness, when attentive observers fail to notice large changes that happen gradually, raises questions about how visual information is combined across time. One plausible integration strategy is serial dependence: blending information from the recent past into current perception. We investigate serial dependencies in perception of a cartoon object that slowly changes hue. In a one-shot experiment, observers each viewed a single trial with a random degree of hue change and provided one hue judgment response. Across participants, the entire morph was probed. Observers' hue reports revealed an overall bias toward the past that increased in magnitude as more of the morph was experienced. In three follow-up experiments, we verified that observers experienced slow change blindness, confirmed that the bias was serial dependence, and replicated the results with a repeated-trials design. Overall, we provide evidence that serial dependence actively biases perception during gradual changes, sometimes producing slow change blindness.

title: Healthcare utilization in patients with spinal disorders referred for specialist evaluation in Norway: an observational register-based cohort study.
abstract: Healthcare utilization is high for people with spinal disorders. We aimed to investigate differences in recommended versus actual healthcare use among individuals with back & neck pain compared to individuals with isolated back or neck pain. Additionally, we aimed to examine variations in healthcare utilization patterns before and after a specialist evaluation based on the location of pain. We linked the Norwegian Neck and Back Registry with health registries, including patients with spinal disorders registered between January 1st, 2016, and December 31st, 2020 (9316 patients (63% with back pain, 27% with neck pain, 11% with back & neck pain) aged 18-70 years, mean (SD) age 44 (13) years, 57% females). We studied the percentages being recommended and actually visiting primary care physicians, physical therapists, and chiropractors in primary care and outpatient and inpatient consultations in specialist care after an outpatient specialist evaluation (index consultation), focusing on differences between groups based on the location of spinal pain. In total, ~20%-80% followed healthcare recommendations. Patients with back & neck pain followed recommendations less often than patients with back pain (39% (95% CI 35.7, 41.8) vs 45% (95% CI 43.9, 46.4)) or neck pain (44% (95% CI 42.4, 46.3)). Participants with back & neck pain had a proportion of consultations with physical therapists at 29.7% (95% CI 25.1, 34.2) and 25.4% (95% CI 20.7, 30.1) in years 1 and 2 after index consultation, ~6 percentage points higher than the back pain group (1st: -5.8% (95% CI -10.6, -1.0), 2nd: -6.0% (95% CI -11.0, -0.9). They also had a 2 percentage point higher proportion of consultations with primary care physicians compared to the neck pain group (1st: -2.4% (95% CI -4.1, -0.8), 2nd: -1.5% (95% CI -2.7, -0.3)). Patients with mixed back & neck pain have lower adherence to recommended care and higher utilization of physical therapy and primary care physicians two years after specialist evaluation compared to patients with isolated spinal pain. These results suggest that the current approach to managing spinal pain should be reconsidered to better address the complex needs of this patient group.

title: The molecular and neurochemical basis of altered intrinsic neural timescales in major depressive disorder: a multimodal imaging-transcriptomic investigation of esketamine and sertraline treatment.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by dysfunction in higher-order cortical regions involved in emotional and cognitive processes; however, its neurobiological basis remains unclear. Pharmacological treatments, including esketamine and sertraline, produce rapid antidepressant effects. We investigated the local intrinsic neural dynamics underlying these antidepressant effects using intrinsic neural timescales (INT), which measure the duration and capacity of information integration in localized brain regions. A total of 57 healthy controls and 41 patients with MDD were included. All patients with MDD received six intravenous infusions of esketamine (0.25 mg/kg) and two weeks of sertraline treatment. All participants underwent resting-state fMRI to quantify INT alterations at the voxel and brain network levels, followed by spatial correlation analyses linking autocorrelation metrics of INT signals to transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas and PET-derived neurotransmitter receptor maps. The spatial correlation between PLS2 scores and case-control t-statistic maps did not pass rigorous spin permutation testing (r = 0.484, p = 0.068) and did not meet the conventional significance threshold of 0.05. Accordingly, all subsequent enrichment analyses based on PLS2 results are presented as exploratory preliminary observations for hypothesis generation. Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD exhibited significantly elevated INT levels in the left and right precuneus. Following treatment, patients with MDD showed significantly increased INT in the left occipital midline region and left calcarine cortex. At the brain network level, INT levels were significantly reduced in the default mode network (DMN) in patients with MDD compared with healthy controls. Compared with the pre-treatment state, the cerebellar network (CN) showed significantly elevated INT levels after treatment. Partial least squares regression analysis suggested potential associations between INT alterations and spatial gene expression gradients particularly those associated with immune responses, hormonal regulation, neutrophils, regulatory T cells, and glutamatergic synapses. Cell-type enrichment analysis identified excitatory and inhibitory neurons as key cellular contributors. Alterations in INT also correlated with cortical 5-HT1b and NAT receptor density, suggesting a role for inhibitory neurotransmission in temporal integration deficits. This study advances understanding of treatment-related brain abnormalities in patients with MDD from the perspective of local neural dynamics. These findings support a multiscale pathophysiological framework involving brain connectivity dynamics, molecular architecture, and neurochemical regulation in MDD.

title: Platelet trajectory patterns and 28-day mortality in ICU stroke patients: a retrospective cohort study based on the MIMIC-IV database.
abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Platelet abnormalities are common in critically ill patients, but dynamic trajectory patterns and their prognostic value in intensive care unit (ICU) stroke patients remain unclear. This retrospective cohort study included 1,562 ICU stroke patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) database (version 3.1). Latent class trajectory models (LCTM) were used to identify platelet trajectory patterns during the first 5 days of ICU admission. Cox proportional hazards regression was performed to assess the association between trajectory groups and 28-day mortality. Exploratory effect decomposition analysis was conducted to explore the relative contribution of baseline platelet levels and subsequent platelet decline to prognosis. Four distinct platelet trajectory groups were identified: High-Declining (14.7%), Moderate-Low Stable (52.4%), Low-Rising (4.5%), and Moderate-High Stable (28.4%). The High-Declining group had the highest 28-day mortality (34.1% vs. 20.4% in the Moderate-Low Stable group, P < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, the High-Declining group was associated with a 56% increase in mortality risk compared with the Moderate-Low Stable group (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.56, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.17-2.07, P = 0.002). Exploratory effect decomposition analysis revealed a suppression pattern: the direct protective effect of higher Day 2 platelet was offset by an indirect harmful effect mediated through greater subsequent platelet decline (Average Component Mediation Effect [ACME] = 0.017 on the probability-difference scale, 95% CI: 0.010-0.026, P < 0.001), suggesting that rapid platelet decline may reflect a high-risk phenotypic pattern associated with this trajectory group. Platelet trajectory patterns are associated with 28-day mortality and may serve as prognostic indicators in ICU stroke patients. A high baseline platelet level with rapid decline represents the highest-risk phenotype and, if confirmed in future prospective studies, may help identify patients requiring closer clinical evaluation to screen for underlying deteriorating conditions.

title: Local infiltration anesthesia combined with S-ketamine for cesarean delivery in a parturient with diaphragmatic hernia and severe scoliosis: a case report.
abstract: Neuraxial and general anesthesia are the conventional approaches for cesarean section. Adjunctive techniques including ultrasonography and video laryngoscopy have further improved the success rate of these anesthetic methods. However, in carefully selected high-risk patients with absolute contraindications to standard techniques, alternative strategies may be considered. We report a case of cesarean delivery performed under local infiltration anesthesia combined with S-ketamine in a pregnant woman with diaphragmatic hernia and severe poliomyelitis-related scoliosis, after all standard anesthetic options were deemed unfeasible or excessively risky. For patients in whom general anesthesia carries prohibitively high risks, neuraxial anesthesia is technically unfeasible, and abdominal regional blocks cannot be performed safely, local infiltration anesthesia with S-ketamine may serve as a last-resort rescue strategy under exceptional circumstances. However, this approach should never be considered an alternative to established anesthetic standards and is only applicable in extremely rare, carefully selected cases.

title: Early loss of axons limits the therapeutic window in a mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy.
abstract: Current treatments for spinal muscular atrophy have significantly improved patient prognosis, but still fall short of a full cure, particularly when administered after symptom onset. To improve future therapies, it is essential to identify the early pathological events that currently limit treatment efficacy. Here we have investigated the vulnerability and maturation of intramuscular motor axons in the SmnΔ7 mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy using a panel of cranial muscles with differing susceptibility to disease. We demonstrate that although there is intermuscular heterogeneity in neuromuscular junction pathology, they are united by a common loss of motor axons. We show that the timing of motor axon loss differs between muscles, but that motor axon loss precedes structural denervation and can occur by postnatal day 1 in highly vulnerable muscles. Electron microscopy of intramuscular axons revealed that axonal maturation and myelination are grossly normal prior to subsequent postnatal degeneration. We note that axons lack the traditional morphological correlates of axon degeneration but can be visualised using antibodies which detect degenerating neurofilaments. Treatment with SMN-upregulating therapy SMN-C8 at best preserves intramuscular axons when administered before the onset of degeneration but is unable to reverse damage or promote regeneration once axon loss has occurred. Collectively this data demonstrates that SMN-upregulating therapy can prevent motor axon loss, but the capacity is limited by the number of intramuscular axons which remain at the time of treatment onset. This work highlights the importance of developing complementary therapies which can promote motor axon regeneration to act in synergy with SMN-upregulating compounds.

title: Dynamic ultrasound assessment of sciatic nerve excursion during neurodynamic mobilizations: a prospective observational study.
abstract: This study evaluates sciatic nerve excursion at the hamstring level during active and passive neurodynamic mobilization (NDM) of the tibial, superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, and sural nerves. The aim is to determine which NDM (active or passive) generates higher excursion. This analytical observational study was carried out at the University Clinic of the University of Manresa over a period of 17 weeks. Participants were placed in a side-lying SLUMP position with 60° of hip flexion and full knee extension. Neurodynamic mobilizations were performed randomly either actively or passively. Simultaneously, sciatic nerve excursion was recorded using high-frequency ultrasound and subsequently quantified using MATLAB software (version 2019b) through a frame-by-frame cross-correlation analysis. Twenty-two participants voluntarily took part in the study (17 women and 5 men), with a mean age of 26.36 ± 6.04 years and a body mass index (BMI) of 22.15 ± 2.78 kg/m2. Mean sciatic nerve excursion during active mobilization was 1.45 ± 0.76 mm, whereas passive mobilization produced an excursion of 1.07 ± 0.74 mm. A statistically significant difference was observed between the two conditions (p < 0.001). The sciatic nerve can be mobilized through its four terminal branches using both active and passive neurodynamic techniques, all of which generate a proximal mechanical effect. Active self-mobilization, particularly through the tibial nerve, may represent an effective therapeutic intervention for patients with proximal sciatic nerve involvement, as it produces greater sciatic nerve excursion at the hamstring level.

title: PAR4 exacerbates intracerebral hemorrhage by driving m6A-dependent microglial AIM2 release and neuronal PANoptosis.
abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a neurological disorder with high morbidity and mortality. PAR4 has been implicated in ICH and neuroinflammation. The rat model of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) was established by injecting collagenase into the brain. TTC staining, H&E staining, and immunofluorescence were used to evaluate the brain tissue. In vitro, rat primary microglia (RPMCs) were isolated and the rat microglial cell line HAPI and the hippocampal neuronal cell line H19-7 were cultured. RNA-seq analysis, Western blot, co-immunoprecipitation, cell immunofluorescence, RIP assay, m6A Dot Blot Analysis were performed to investigate the role of PAR4 and its downstream signaling pathways. In the ICH rat model, treatment with the PAR4 antagonist inhibited neuronal death and reversed the M1-dominant shift of microglia. PAR4 regulated m6A methylation in microglia via KIAA1429-mediated recruitment of methyltransferase complexes. PAR4AP increased JAK2 mRNA m6A modification, mRNA and protein levels, and enhanced STAT3 protein phosphorylation. It also increased the expression of inflammatory factors and inflammasome components, with a stronger effect on AIM2 expression. PAR4AP enhanced AIM2 expression in microglial cells through mechanisms dependent on the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway and m6A modification. PAR4AP-activated microglia induce neuronal PANoptosis via exosome-mediated transfer of AIM2, promoting Pyrin-ZBP1 complex formation. In a rat model of ICH, lentivirus-delivered shRNAs targeting KIAA1429, FMR1, and AIM2, as well as PAR4 inhibition, suppressed PANoptosis in neuronal cells. This study provides insights into the role of PAR4 in ICH and its downstream signaling pathways, suggesting potential therapeutic targets for ICH treatment.

title: The Future of Targeted Degradation: Outlook and Unanswered Questions.
abstract: By hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome system to catalytically degrade pathogenic proteins, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) offers unprecedented opportunities to eliminate intractable targets, dismantle scaffolding functions, and achieve deeper, more durable therapeutic responses. This chapter provides a forward-looking examination of the field, moving beyond proof-of-concept to address the critical chemical, biological, and translational questions that will define the next decade. We dissect the evolution of degrader design, from expanding the ligand toolbox to target previously "undruggable" proteins, to engineering programmable degradation platforms with spatiotemporal and logic-gated control. A central focus is placed on the deep integration of artificial intelligence, which is reshaping rational design by predicting ternary complex dynamics and ubiquitin transfer efficiency. Crucially, we confront the translational conundrums head-on, analyzing the unique pharmacokinetic /pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationships, the multi-layered mechanisms of acquired resistance, and the dual nature of collateral degradation in the context of therapeutic safety. By bridging state-of-the-art medicinal chemistry with clinical pharmacology, we delineate a roadmap for harnessing this transformative modality to deliver on its promise for patients, particularly in oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration.

title: Author Correction: mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis.
Meet Neuropixels: how probes that track hundreds of brain cells at once are revolutionizing neuroscience.
The nanotubular network as a new dimension of intercellular communication in the nervous system.
abstract: Communication between cells in the nervous system has long been understood to occur through chemical and electrical synapses, and through the release of signalling molecules and extracellular vesicles across the extracellular space. Intercellular nanotubes (NTs) - thin, membranous tubular bridges that physically connect distant cells - represent a structurally distinct route of communication, enabling the direct, targeted transfer of cellular cargoes between selected cells. Once studied almost exclusively in culture, NTs have now been visualized in situ and in vivo throughout the nervous system, including dendritic NTs between neurons, NTs formed by microglia and astrocytes, interpericyte NTs in the retina and NTs between satellite glia and peripheral sensory neurons. Through these connections, cells exchange mitochondria, proteins and their aggregates, and calcium, supporting three emerging roles: homeostatic rescue of stressed cells, pathological propagation of toxic proteins in neurodegeneration and non-synaptic calcium signalling, respectively. NT networks are dynamic and stress-responsive, suggesting that they provide a plastic infrastructure for resource sharing among neurons and glia. Understanding their function will require establishing a standardized definition, achieving rigorous in situ validation and quantification, and developing specific molecular tools to manipulate NTs.

title: Sleep-sensitive neurons mediate consolidation.
Amyloid beta governs mitochondrial lipid metabolism defects and neurodegenerative lysosomal stress.
abstract: Mechanisms linking amyloid peptides to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain poorly defined. Here, we report that, in healthy aging neurons, mitochondrial ceramide synthase 1 (CerS1) localization accompanies increased mitochondrial C18-ceramide and mitophagy in damaged mitochondria. In neuronal, mouse, and human AD tissues, amyloid precursor protein (APP) or Aβ40, but not Aβ42, shows increased proximity or co-association with TOM20/TOM40 alongside reduced mitochondrial CerS1/C18-ceramide accumulation and mitophagy. Mitochondria-excluded mutant APP does not reproduce these responses in neuronal cells. WT-APP expression is associated with reduced p17/PERMIT-ICT1 proximity, which does not establish direct APP-ICT1 binding or disruption of complex formation. Reduced mitophagy also accompanies lysosomal Aβ42 accumulation and secretion from neurons. Aged CerS1top/top mice, expressing catalytically inactive CerS1, exhibit mitochondrial dysfunction, behavioral deficits, and amyloid-positive plaque accumulation. Treatment with the peptide-targeted nanoparticle Pen-Cera-LCL768, which accumulates in the brain after intranasal administration, increases mitophagy-related readouts, reduces plaque burden, and improves behavioral performance in aged 3xTg and CerS1top/top mice. Mdivi-1 attenuates treatment effects in 3xTg mice, but its lack of specificity limits conclusions about mitophagy dependence.

title: Flower isoforms mediate fitness selection of astrocytes through extracellular vesicles.
abstract: Cellular fitness surveillance preserves tissue integrity by eliminating less-fit cells, yet its regulation within the complex glial networks of the mammalian brain remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a dual-domain mechanism in the transmembrane protein Flower-which encodes survival-promoting ("win") and apoptosis-inducing ("lose") isoforms-that enables non-contact-dependent fitness signaling in astrocytes. We show that astrocytes release extracellular vesicles (EVs) carrying full-length Flower, allowing for intercellular surveillance between distant cells. The shared N-terminal domain acts extrinsically via EVs to drive the elimination of distal, less-fit cells. In contrast, the C-terminal domain,exclusive to the win isoform,functions intrinsically independent of EV transport; it translocates to the nucleus to downregulate caspase-3 and enhance survival. In APP-transgenic mice and human Alzheimer's disease brains, Flower-positive astrocytes accumulate around amyloid-β plaques. Under amyloid-β stress, the win isoform promotes a neuroprotective reactive state that enhances plaque clearance. Our findings reveal how Flower couples EV-mediated attack signals with intrinsic nuclear protection to coordinate astrocyte quality control and tissue resilience in neurodegeneration.

title: Endogenous rhythms in deep-sea mussel cell culture and molecular clock characterization.
abstract: While biological rhythms are crucial to life, the deep sea has long been considered an arrhythmic exception. However, at hydrothermal vents - devoid of diel cues yet shaped by tides - the mussel Bathymodiolus azoricus shows both tidal and, unexpectedly, circadian rhythms at -1700 m. Whether endogenous clock(s) drive these cycles remained unanswered. Here, we report endogenous circadian rhythms in B. azoricus cell cultures under constant conditions: isolated cells display a circadian oscillation despite tidal-dominant rhythms in the natural environment. Reporter assays using genomic regions upstream of the mussel's per gene and containing E-box motifs suggest that a functional transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) contributes to circadian timing even in the deep sea. In mussels, BazPeriod lacks autonomous repressive activity but modulates BazCry2. As BazPeriod itself oscillates tidally, it may explain how a single endogenous clock yields both tidal and diel rhythms. The work also spotlights the highly time-sensitive biology of the vastly unexplored deep-sea environment.

title: Misfolded tau propagates via templated seeding.
It's time to split.
Correcting automatic decisions.
A brain of many microglia origins.
Peripheral neuroimmune dialogues underlying pain states.
abstract: Pain is profoundly shaped by neuroimmune interactions within peripheral tissues. Nociceptors are specialized sensory neurons that express receptors for cytokines, lipid mediators, complement components, antibodies and microbial signals, enabling immune mediators to directly modulate neuronal excitability. In turn, nociceptors influence immune cell and stromal cell activity through the release of neuropeptides and cytokines. Some of these pathways are shared across multiple tissues in pathological pain states, whereas others reflect the distinct immune and stromal environments of the skin, joints, muscles, gut, peripheral nerves, sensory ganglia and meninges. Across these sites, immune-to-neuron signalling orchestrates the initiation and amplification of pain, while maladaptive feedback loops reinforce hypersensitivity. In concert, coordinated neuroimmune signalling also contributes to pain resolution by restoring homeostasis. Emerging human studies reveal convergent neuroimmune signatures across nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain conditions, underscoring their translational relevance. By integrating both shared mechanisms and tissue-specific mechanisms, this Review highlights how peripheral neuroimmune crosstalk shapes pain across diverse contexts. Furthermore, it outlines therapeutic opportunities to rebalance these pathways, offering prospects for durable and mechanism-based analgesia.

title: The Royal College of Ophthalmologists' National Ophthalmology Database: report 15, severe vision loss following cataract surgery.
abstract: To investigate rates of severe vision loss post-cataract surgery. Post-cataract severe vision loss (SVL) was defined as a loss of ≥0.60 LogMAR between preoperative presenting visual acuity and postoperative visual acuity. The term 'legally blind' was used for eyes with a corrected visual acuity worse than 1.30 LogMAR. Between 2010 and 2024, there were 1,750,553 eligible operations performed on 1,217,267 patients by 3766 surgeons from 132 centres supplying data to the Royal College of Ophthalmologists National Ophthalmology Database Cataract Audit. Severe vision loss was recorded in 3723 (0.21%) eyes, including 3 eyes (2 patients) from 2 718 immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery (ISBCS) eyes. The highest observed SVL rate was 10.68% for eyes recorded as left aphakic after surgery and the second highest observed SVL rate (3.32%) was when posterior capsular rupture occurred. The SVL rate was higher than the overall rate for eyes with previous intravitreal injections (0.76%), eyes with optic nerve or central nervous system problems (0.74%), age-related macular degeneration (0.52%), previous vitrectomy surgery (0.49%), diabetic retinopathy (0.45%), glaucoma (0.42%) or corneal pathology (0.33%). Of 1,642,386 (93.8%) eyes that were not preoperatively legally blind, 2731 (0.2%) were postoperatively legally blind. Of these, 2294 (84.0%) eyes experienced severe vision loss. Severe vision loss from any cause following cataract surgery occurs infrequently. However, it has a higher prevalence in eyes left aphakic, when PCR occurs and for certain ocular comorbidities.

title: Publisher Correction: Network geometry shapes the transformation of task representations across the human cortex.
A multi-institutional investigation of psilocybin's effects on mouse behavior.
abstract: Studies reporting the effects of psychedelic drugs on mouse behavior are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these effects remain uncertain. Here we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to assess which effects of psilocybin on mouse behavior are robust and replicable. Five independent laboratories performed the same experiments to test the acute and persistent effects of psilocybin (2 mg kg-1, intraperitoneally) on various behaviors. Psilocybin acutely increased anxiety- and avoidance-related behaviors and decreased fear expression in a robust and replicable manner. Surprisingly, however, psilocybin did not have replicable effects 24 h after administration in terms of reducing anxiety- and depression-like behaviors or facilitating fear extinction learning. Additionally, we did not observe psilocybin-induced alterations in social preference or social reward learning. Our characterization of psilocybin's behavioral effects, using ~200 male and female mice per experiment across five laboratories, demonstrates several robust acute effects and suggests that some of psilocybin's reported persistent effects in mice may be modest and/or inconsistent.

title: Real-time geometric complexity of language is associated with global functioning across psychosis and major depression.
abstract: Language disturbances are prominent across psychiatric disorders, yet their underlying organization and relationship to clinical functioning remain poorly understood. We conceptualized spontaneous speech as a temporally evolving sequence of contextual representations through semantic space, in which successive concepts define transitions between large-language-model embeddings. We characterized the local dynamics of these representations using Lyapunov-inspired measures of sensitivity to perturbation and anisotropy-the extent to which nearby neighboring contextual representations diverge differently depending on direction in representational space. We applied this approach to picture descriptions from 129 German-speaking participants with major depressive disorder (n = 43), schizophrenia spectrum disorders (n = 42), or no psychiatric diagnosis (n = 44). Individual differences in local geometric dynamics predicted multiple clinical dimensions, with the strongest association observed for global functioning, for which the geometric measures explained 51% of the variance. Clinically informative geometric structure was already detectable within the first three sentences of speech, where distinct dynamical profiles were associated with differences in negative and positive symptoms, anxiety, depression, and global functioning. These associations suggest that the dynamics of local representational divergence and contraction during speech reflect broad variation in cognitive and social functioning rather than diagnosis alone. Together, these findings suggest that psychiatric variation is reflected not simply in what people say, but in the dynamics by which semantic representations evolve during ongoing language production. A dynamical-geometric analysis of language may provide a compact, transdiagnostic marker of clinically meaningful variation in psychopathology.

title: Serum selenium, iron and rubidium are altered in treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
abstract: The molecular basis of schizophrenia is complex, involving an interplay of genetic and environmental factors. In recent postmortem and imaging studies, we identified disturbances in iron homeostasis in cortical and subcortical regions of individuals with schizophrenia. These may be relevant to neuropathology identified in the disorder and could relate to mechanisms of oxidative stress and inflammation. Recent work has proposed that there is a dysregulation of brain metals and other elements in schizophrenia that might impact on oxidative stress. Using a metallomics approach, we report robust changes in serum levels of pro-oxidant iron, anti-oxidant selenium, and the potassium-marker, rubidium, in a cohort of people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS). The cohort also expressed elevated levels of serum pro-inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin, and lower levels of anti-oxidant selenoproteins, selenoprotein-P1 (SEPP1) and glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3). The changes in serum iron, rubidium and selenium discriminate between control individuals and TRS cases, and they were not affected by age or clozapine serum levels. We propose that the changes in selenium and cytokines might drive the expression of hepcidin, resulting in reduced serum iron levels. Further research should investigate the relationship between peripheral and central measures of these elements and their metabolism, and further explore the relevance of pro-oxidant stress to the neuropathology of schizophrenia.

title: Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder.
abstract: Although antidepressants remain the main pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), therapeutic response varies, highlighting the need for molecular markers that predict treatment response, as well as insights into the biological processes underlying antidepressant efficacy. Candidate-gene and cross-sectional epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have reported DNA methylation signatures associated with antidepressant response; however, findings remain inconsistent. To date, no longitudinal EWAS has examined methylation trajectories across multiple time points during antidepressant treatment in MDD. Within the Early Medication Change trial, DNA methylation data was generated for 162 patients with MDD (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 matched healthy controls. Patients were assessed at four times across eight-weeks of standardized antidepressant treatment, while controls were assessed twice. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and regions (DMRs) were identified using longitudinal EWAS models and the comb-p algorithm. Baseline methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56 through two and six DMRs, respectively (e.g., TNRC6C, CAT), whereas no single DMP reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP associated with improvement in depressive symptoms (YLMP1) and three DMRs showing methylation changes over time (e.g., GPR126, PM20D1). Combined patient-control analyses revealed additional DMPs and DMRs associated with diagnosis and temporal effects. This study provides first longitudinal evidence of regionally coordinated DNA methylation changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy, revealing alterations in genes involved in neuroplasticity and inflammatory processes that are associated with clinical response. Replication and functional validation will be essential to determine their relevance for personalized antidepressant treatment.

title: Clinical, neuroimaging, and longitudinal progression characteristics of GBA1-associated Parkinson's disease in a Northeast China cohort.
abstract: GBA1 is a common genetic risk factor for Parkinson's disease (PD), but PET/CT and longitudinal data in Chinese populations remain limited. We aimed to determine the frequency of GBA1-associated PD (GBA1-PD) in Northeast China and compare its clinical features, PET/CT images, and 3-year progression with non-GBA1-associated PD (NGBA1-PD). In this single-center observational cohort, 301 patients with PD underwent whole-exome sequencing, orthogonal validation and clinical assessment; 176 underwent 11C-CFT and 18F-FDG PET/CT, and 271 completed follow-up. GBA1 variants were identified in 25 patients (8.31%). Compared with NGBA1-PD, GBA1-PD showed greater motor and cognitive impairment, higher PIGD proportion, worse sleep-related symptoms, lower striatal 11C-CFT uptake, and lower metabolism in the precuneus. Over 3 years, GBA1-PD showed trends toward faster motor and mood deterioration, although these differences did not remain significant after FDR correction. These findings suggest distinct clinical and imaging features of GBA1-PD and potential value for prognostic stratification. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: A serotonergic mechanism is involved in the pro-cognitive effect of AM6545 treatment in a mouse model of fragile X syndrome.
abstract: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the principal monogenic syndrome leading to inherited intellectual disability and autism. It is caused by the silencing of FMR1 gene that leads to the loss in the expression of its encoded protein, the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMRP). In synapses, FMRP has a key role in local mRNA modulation to maintain synaptic plasticity. The Fmr1 KO (FX) mouse model shows cognitive impairment and some of the synaptic traits present in individuals with FXS, together with alterations in gut microbiota. Previous studies revealed that pharmacological and genetic cannabinoid type-1 receptor (CB1R) inhibition significantly prevented central key alterations in FX mice. Here, we aimed to evaluate the effect of a sub-chronic treatment with the largely peripherally-restricted CB1R antagonist AM6545. We found that AM6545 reduced memory deficits and restored enhanced hippocampal mGluR5-dependent long-term depression and aberrant dendritic spine density in FX mice. At the peripheral level, AM6545 modified altered FX mice fecal microbiota composition and intestinal Muc2 expression, while in the hippocampus AM6545 treatment upregulated hippocampal Htr4, the gene encoding for serotonin receptor 4 (5-HT4R). This upregulation, also observed in cecum, positively correlated with memory performance. Notably, acute pharmacological blockade of 5-HT4R abolished AM6545 pro-cognitive effect. Our results suggest that repeated peripheral CB1R inhibition ameliorates key central and peripheral alterations in FXS mouse model and modifies the expression of serotonergic receptors important for cognitive performance. Together, this evidence points to the peripheral targeting of CB1R as an approach to alleviate cognitive dysfunction in the FXS context.

title: Beyond the scars: current understanding of risk factors, neurobiological mechanisms and effective interventions for non-suicidal self-injury in young adults.
abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is highly prevalent in adolescents and young adults. However, NSSI in young adulthood remains understudied despite this developmental stage is characterized by increading life demands, social transitions, and ongoing brain maturation. This manuscript synthesizes current evidence on risk factors, neurobiology, and treatments for NSSI in emerging adults. Emotional dysregulation, rumination and impulsivity emerge as core individual vulnerabilities, often interacting with adverse childhood experiences and interpersonal stressors. Conversely, perceived social support and metacognitive capacity serve as protective factors. Neurobiological findings, although limited, implicate genetic and epigenetic alongside structural and functional brain abnormalities. Neuroimaging studies reveal that young adults with NSSI exhibit intact nocioceptive encoding but attenuated affective pain responses, together with abnormal recruitment of striatal-midbrin reward pathways. Furthermore, evidence indicates disrupted frontolimbic connectivity underlying emotion regulation deficits and altered self-other processing within medial prefrontal and temporoparietal networks. Treatment research focused on young adults is limited. The Treatment for Sel-Injurious Behaviors (T-SIB) represents the only age-specific intervention with preliminary efficacy evidence. Future research should prioritize young adult samples to clarify the neurobiological mechanisms of NSSI in this critical developmental period and to develop more accessible and effective interventions.

title: Human cortico-vascular assembloids reveal a CELF2-AHNAK-dependent switch from neuronal to endothelial tropism in glioblastoma cells.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive human cancers, driven by cellular plasticity and dynamic interactions with the neurovascular niche. Yet, further refinement of existing preclinical models is needed to improve the reproduction of the human brain-vascular interface and facilitate the study of tumor-host crosstalk and invasion. To address this limitation, we developed a human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived cortico-endothelial (CO + EO) assembloid model by fusing cortical and endothelial organoids. These assembloids spontaneously form branched vascular networks enriched in tight junction proteins (CLDN5, OCLN, ZO-1), thereby recapitulating key BBB-like features and providing a physiologically relevant human platform to investigate GBM-neurovascular interactions. Using this system, we uncovered a previously unrecognized CELF2-dependent glioma stem cell (GSC) tropism. CELF2-expressing GSCs preferentially infiltrate neural regions, where they induce neuronal apoptosis and disrupt endothelial tight junction structure, supporting an aggressive phenotype. In contrast, CELF2-deficient GSCs lose neurotropism, acquire mesenchymal features, and are redirected toward vascular compartments. This endothelial affinity depends on the scaffold protein AHNAK, strongly expressed at the plasma membrane of CELF2-deficient cells and enriched at tumor-endothelial interfaces. AHNAK knockdown partially abolishes endothelial infiltration, demonstrating its role in GBM vascular tropism. Moreover, analysis of patient GBM specimens confirmed that CELF2-positive tumor cells are enriched in poorly vascularized, mitotically active regions and are largely excluded from vessel-rich zones, closely resembling the behavior observed in assembloids. Transcriptomic profiling further revealed that CELF2 promotes a neuronal progenitor-like program while repressing mesenchymal and vascular-associated gene signatures, thereby shaping tumor identity, invasive behavior, and tissue preference. Collectively, this study establishes CO + EO assembloids as an original human model of GBM plasticity at the neurovascular interface. We identify CELF2 as a master regulator of GSC tropism and AHNAK as a mediator of vascular affinity, revealing a molecular axis that governs GBM invasion and providing potential avenues for future therapeutic intervention. Schematic representation of CO + EO assembloids comprising an endothelial (yellow) and a cortical (red) domain. On the left, control CELF2-expressing GBM cells preferentially infiltrate the neuronal compartment, where they trigger neuronal apoptosis and disrupt the expression of the tight junction protein CLDN5 upon contact with endothelial cells. On the right, CELF2-deprived GBM cells exhibit reduced neural invasion and increased tropism for endothelial cells, consistent with a mesenchymal signature shift partially driven by elevated AHNAK expression. These cells exert limited impact on neuronal viability and BBB integrity, and display partial loss of GSC identity, as indicated by reduced OLIG2 expression. The CO + EO assembloid model thus recapitulates key features of cortico-endothelial human tissue heterogeneity and provides a reliable platform to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying GSC tropism and their tissue-specific interactions.

title: Adolescent environmental enrichment prevents early-life stress-induced schizophrenia-like phenotypes via restoration of CREB-BDNF-TrkB signaling.
abstract: Early-life stress (ELS) is a major environmental risk factor for schizophrenia, yet effective preventive strategies targeting its neurodevelopmental consequences remain limited. Here, we show that adolescent environmental enrichment (EE) prevents the emergence of schizophrenia-like behavioral and cognitive deficits induced by maternal separation (MS), a validated ELS model. Mechanistically, MS induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and synaptic deficits in the hippocampus, accompanied by suppression of the CREB-BDNF-TrkB (cAMP response element-binding protein-brain-derived neurotrophic factor-tropomyosin receptor kinase B) signaling. Adolescent EE robustly reversed these abnormalities and restored neuroplasticity-related signaling. Importantly, we provide evidence supporting a causal role of TrkB signaling in these protective effects within the experimental framework used here: pharmacological activation of TrkB rescued oxidative stress-induced synaptic deficits in vitro, whereas pharmacological inhibition of TrkB abolished the behavioral and cognitive benefits of EE in vivo. To establish translational relevance, we further show that TrkB levels are significantly reduced in neuron-derived exosomes (NDEs) from patients with schizophrenia, with moderate diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.784). Together, these findings support CREB-BDNF-TrkB signaling as a key mechanistic node linking ELS to schizophrenia-related phenotypes and suggest adolescent EE as a developmentally timed, non-pharmacological intervention with translational relevance within the experimental framework used here.

title: Orthosteric and allosteric inhibition of the brain V-ATPase outside the alternating-access cycle.
abstract: Active transporters move solutes uphill by harnessing the free energy stored in ATP or ion-motive gradients. A central tenet of molecular pharmacology is that orthosteric and allosteric inhibitors of active transporters act by slowing the transport cycle. We test this foundational premise, previously supported by ensemble-average data, at the single-molecule level. Using endogenous mammalian-brain V-ATPase, we show that bulk acidification can be abolished without any reduction in the single-molecule proton-transport rate. Instead, inhibitors predominantly promote reversible excursions outside the canonical transport cycle into ultralong-lived inactive modes. Overall, our findings establish the existence of two orthogonal axes of pharmacological control (on-cycle catalytic rates and off-cycle mode occupancy) that can be selectively or jointly actuated for precision drug design and likely generalize to other active transporters.

title: RhoA Y42C drives cell plasticity and PD-1-mediated immune evasion of diffuse gastric cancer.
abstract: Diffuse gastric cancer (DGC) is an aggressive gastric cancer subtype with a poor prognosis. The RHOA Y42C mutation is recurrent in DGC, but its independent oncogenic role is unclear. Next-Generation Sequencing of 431 DGC cases revealed that most RHOA mutations occurred without CDH1 alterations. Using genetically engineered gastric organoids, we show that RhoaY42C, along with KrasG12D and Trp53 loss (RKP), induces DGC, independently of Cdh1 loss. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal that RKP tumors exhibit mucinous histopathology and a specific lineage trajectory from Aqp5+ cells to Muc1/Muc4+ cells. RKP tumors create an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment where AREG, transactivated by RhoA Y42C-YAP1, causes T cell exhaustion via PD-1 upregulation. Unlike E-cadherin loss-associated DGC, RKP tumors are highly susceptible to PD-1 blockade. Additionally, the RHOA Y42C mutation correlates with PD-1 upregulation in human DGC samples. These findings redefine the oncogenic role of RhoA Y42C, confirming its sufficiency for DGC development and suggesting PD-1 inhibition as a viable therapeutic option for DGC patients carrying this mutation.

title: Sexually dimorphic control of excitatory synapse maintenance in ventral hippocampal circuits by Neurexin2α ligand Vstm2b.
abstract: Neuronal networks rely on precise synapse formation, maturation, and maintenance orchestrated by synaptic adhesion molecules including α- and β-neurexins (Nrxns). Through unbiased proteomics, we identified Vstm2 family members as α-Nrxn-specific interactors that require inclusion of an insert at alternative splice site 2 (SS2) in α-Nrxns. In particular, as a selective ligand of axonal Nrxn2αSS2+, Vstm2b promotes glutamatergic presynaptic assembly. Loss of Vstm2b in mice impairs glutamatergic synaptic function and maintenance in the ventral hippocampal CA1 (vCA1), while leaving early synaptogenesis intact. These impairments are sex- and input-specific, highlighting distinct circuit vulnerabilities in male and female mice. Accordingly, Vstm2b knockout mice exhibit sexually dimorphic anxiety-related behaviors and social deficits. Our findings establish the Vstm2b-Nrxn2α synaptic adhesion complex as a critical regulator of vCA1 excitatory synapse stability and functional organization and reveal the α-Nrxn-centered interactome as a key driver of sex-dependent synaptic specificity and circuit functions that underlie social behavior and anxiety.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR-screening identifies p53 as regulator of cancer cell sensitivity to the histone evicting anthracycline aclarubicin.
abstract: The anthracycline family, with its prime member doxorubicin, is one of the cornerstones in cancer chemotherapy and acts by poisoning topoisomerase II, resulting in DNA double-stranded breaks. One of its members, aclarubicin, is considered a distinct member of this family due to its inability to inflict DNA double-strand breaks. Despite this, aclarubicin is an effective anti-cancer drug by evicting histones, resulting in chromatin damage. How aclarubicin-induced chromatin damage induces cell death remains largely unknown. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR screen to identify factors regulating sensitivity of cells to aclarubicin and identified p53 as a critical factor for cellular sensitivity. Even though aclarubicin does not induce DNA breaks, treatment resulted in swift activation of ATM independent of the MRN complex, which stabilized and activated p53, resulting in apoptosis and cell cycle arrest. Furthermore, response to aclarubicin treatment could reasonably be predicted by the p53-status of cell lines. These data suggest that ATM and p53 can be activated for apoptosis induction by at least two different pathways, DNA- and chromatin damage. Together, these data suggest p53 could be an important factor to stratify patients for treatment with Aclarubicin.
keywords: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats

title: Electronically tuned N-terminal glycine selective bioconjugation enables in vitro and in vivo species-specific Staphylococcus aureus targeting.
abstract: Precisely targeting a biomolecule within living systems could create unique opportunities at the biology-medicine interface. Such methods have been non-trivial due to the complex selectivity attributes. Here, we introduce an electronically tunable chemical technology that targets N-terminal glycine, a unique low-frequency molecular signature. Initially, we established the method using peptides and proteins, along with mechanistic insights. The reactivity, selectivity, and bioconjugate stability remain unaffected by diverse bioadditives. These unique attributes enable the selective targeting of the pentaglycine-based molecular signature in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), a leading contributor to bacterial infection-associated mortality. Notably, the method facilitates species-specific detection of S. aureus and its resistant strains. It enables late-stage bond-engineering to install multiple biorthogonal handles, downstream chemistry, and chemically orthogonal reversal. The specificity extends to in vivo labeling of S. aureus within Drosophila melanogaster, as well as skin, tissue, and blood infections in mice. The N-terminal glycine modification inhibits drug-susceptible and drug-resistant clinical strains of S. aureus, including biofilm formation and preformed biofilms. Finally, the in vivo efficiency is established using a wound-healing assay in mice. The exclusive N-terminal glycine residue-specific targeting across the molecular complexity spectrum, both in vitro and in vivo, establishes peptidoglycan as a potential diagnostic and therapeutic target.

title: Nanobody-Modified Outer Membrane Vesicles Attenuate Alzheimer's Disease-Like Neurodegeneration by Modulating Mitophagy-Associated Phenotypes and cGAS-STING-Related Inflammatory Signaling.
abstract: This study examined anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) nanobody-functionalized bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) as an engineered platform for improving Alzheimer's disease (AD)-like neuronal injury. Escherichia coli-derived OMVs were characterized for morphology, size distribution, surface charge, protein features, nanobody loading, residual endotoxin levels, endotoxin-associated inflammatory responses, and repeated-exposure immune-safety readouts, and were evaluated in neuronal-related cells and APP/PS1 mice. Engineered OMVs showed receptor-associated uptake and preferential brain-delivery signals, increased HT-22 cell viability, reduced apoptosis, and elevated mitophagy-associated markers including LC3-II, PINK1, and Parkin. OMV treatment also reduced cytosolic mtDNA abundance, DNA/cGAS colocalization, phosphorylation of STING/TBK1/IRF3, and inflammatory-marker expression. PINK1 or Parkin knockdown partially weakened OMV-associated mitochondrial and inflammatory readouts, whereas pharmacological autophagy modulation supported a contribution of autophagy-related processes without establishing selective PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy in vivo. In APP/PS1 mice, OMV administration improved Morris water maze and rotarod performance and alleviated neuroinflammatory and histological injury-related changes. Overall, anti-TfR nanobody-modified OMVs were associated with enhanced receptor-related delivery, mitophagy-linked phenotypes, reduced cytosolic mtDNA/cGAS-STING-related inflammatory signaling, and improved AD-like outcomes, supporting further delivery-system optimization and mechanistic validation.

title: Ending Another Successful Year for GSJ.
IL-33 modulates maternal-fetal macrophage immunometabolism and is associated with attenuation of MIA-associated behavioral abnormalities in adult offspring.
abstract: Maternal immune activation (MIA) is a pivotal risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder. However, the mechanisms of MIA at the maternal-fetal interface remain elusive. Here, we used soluble tachyzoite antigen (STAg) from Toxoplasma gondii to induce MIA in pregnant mice at E14.5, followed by maternal administration of interleukin-33 (IL-33) from E15.5 to E17.5. Proteomic profiling coupled with protein-protein interaction network analysis nominated IL-33 as a candidate immunoregulatory factor. In exploratory analyses, maternal IL-33 administration was associated with shifts in macrophage-associated immune profiles, reduced placental inflammation, and attenuated MIA-associated behavioral abnormalities in adult offspring. Given that suppression of tumorigenicity 2 (ST2) is the cognate receptor for IL-33, we next interrogated this pathway in ST2-deficient mice. ST2 deficiency abolished the effects of IL-33 on macrophage repolarization and inflammatory homeostasis, and the behavioral improvements were not evident in ST2-deficient offspring. Mechanistically, IL-33 administration was associated with reduced glycolytic features and improved mitochondrial function in macrophages, consistent with partial restoration of immunometabolic homeostasis at the maternal-fetal interface. Collectively, our findings highlight an immunometabolic axis in STAg-induced MIA pathogenesis, revealing IL-33/ST2 signaling as a potential experimental target for mitigating MIA-associated immune and behavioral abnormalities.

title: Plasma short-chain fatty acids and risk of cardiovascular events and recurrent stroke after ischemic stroke.
journal: Nutrition, metabolism, and cardiovascular diseases : NMCD
abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) serve as important mediators linking the gut microbiome to ischemic stroke and are associated with poststroke recovery and neuronal plasticity. However, population-based prognostic evidence for circulating SCFAs after ischemic stroke is scarce. We aimed to evaluate the relationships between multiple SCFAs and cardiovascular events in patients with ischemic stroke. We conducted a nested case-control study within the China Antihypertensive Trial in Acute Ischemic Stroke with 328 cardiovascular events and 328 controls, matched for age, sex and treatment group. The primary outcome was cardiovascular events after ischemic stroke. Nine plasma SCFAs were determined by ultra-high-performance LC-MS/MS. Logistic regression models were applied to incremental predictive value of SCFAs were evaluated. We identified 6 SCFAs (acetate, isobutyrate, isovalerate, caproate, isocaproate and 3-hydroxyisovalerate) that were inversely associated with cardiovascular events, with multivariable-adjusted ORs per 1 log-SD increment ranging from 0.31 to 0.53 (all P values < 0.05). Acetate, caproate and 3-hydroxyisovalerate were also associated with recurrent stroke, with the multivariable-adjusted ORs ranging from 0.30 to 0.37. The SCFAs score constructed by 6 identified SCFAs was associated with both cardiovascular events and recurrent stroke, ORs (95% CIs) for the highest versus lowest tertile were 0.49 (0.32-0.77) and 0.49 (0.30-0.80), respectively. Furthermore, the SCFAs score offered substantially predictive capability for cardiovascular events and recurrent stroke, beyond traditional risk factors and clinical features. Higher SCFAs were associated with lower risks of cardiovascular events and recurrent stroke after ischemic stroke, and provided incremental value for risk discrimination and reclassification after ischemic stroke.

title: Focused Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease: From Mechanisms to Precision Therapy.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that markedly impairs motor function and quality of life. As conventional pharmacotherapy and deep brain stimulation are increasingly limited by waning efficacy, treatment-related complications or surgical ineligibility, focused ultrasound (FUS) has emerged as a versatile, non-invasive platform that delivers acoustic energy with high spatiotemporal precision. Prior investigations of FUS for PD have often remained fragmented within two largely disconnected domains: clinical application and laboratory-based mechanistic validation. To bridge the gap between these two disconnected domains, a narrative and translational review was conducted that integrates the latest advances from both fields into a unified framework. A structured literature search of PubMed and Web of Science for articles published between January 2004 and November 2025 was conducted. After applying pre-defined inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria, a total of 114 articles were identified and constitute the evidence base for this review. Reference lists of included articles were manually screened to identify additional relevant publications. Our findings critically benchmark thermal ablation, transcranial ultrasound stimulation and BBB opening against established therapies, while appraising their key technical limitations. Looking forward, this review highlights three engineering trajectories poised to propel the field from empirical trial-and-error toward precision medicine: predictive numerical simulations for individualized treatment planning, standardization of sonication protocols and regulatory frameworks, and the evolution from open-loop to real-time closed-loop intelligent control for personalized adaptive therapy. By integrating mechanistic insights, clinical evidence and emerging technologies, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for advancing FUS-based precision management of PD.

title: Visual, hearing, and dual sensory impairment and risk of dementia: The role of social isolation, depressive symptoms, and cognitive function.
abstract: Sensory impairment (SI), including visual impairment (VI), hearing impairment (HI), and dual sensory impairment (DSI), is common in aging adults and associated with increased dementia risk. Older adults with SI often have poorer cognition, a predictor of dementia. We investigated associations of VI, HI, and DSI with incident dementia while accounting for baseline cognition, and assessed indirect pathways through cognition, social isolation, and depressive symptoms. 51,584 UK biobank participants aged 60-70 years with objectively measured visual and hearing function were followed for incident dementia for a mean of 12.1 years. VI was defined as visual acuity worse than 0.30 LogMAR in better-seeing eye; HI as speech-reception threshold in noise greater than -5.5 dB; DSI as both VI and HI. Cognition was assessed using pairs matching and reaction time tests. Dementia was ascertained through linked medical records and death registries RESULTS: After adjustment for cognition and covariates, VI, HI, and DSI remained associated with increased incident dementia risk. Direct-effect HRs were 1.33 for VI, 1.37 for HI, and 2.21 for DSI (all p < 0.05). VI, HI and DSI were also indirectly associated with dementia through depressive symptoms, social isolation, and cognition. The total indirect effect of DSI through all mediators increased dementia risk by 10.5%. VI, HI, and DSI were associated with dementia risk through direct and indirect pathways. Findings support prevention and treatment of VI and HI as potentially modifiable dementia risk factors, and highlight integrated sensory, cognitive, and psychosocial approaches for dementia prevention and healthy aging.

title: Atrophy-Robust Multiclass CNN Segmentation of Brainstem-Related Structures in Neurodegenerative Parkinson Syndromes.
abstract: Neurodegenerative Parkinson syndromes show regionally distinct tissue loss involving several brainstem and midbrain structures. Reliable volumetry is constrained by atlas-based segmentation in atrophy-affected brains. We developed a multiclass convolutional neural network (CNN) for the segmentation of 16 brainstem-related regions on routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). In this retrospective single-center study, 200 manually annotated MRI datasets of patients with Parkinson's disease, atypical Parkinson syndromes, and healthy controls were used for model development and validation. A Deep Neural Patchwork model was trained on 150 datasets and evaluated in an independent test cohort of 50 participants against atlas-based segmentation using the Dice coefficient, 95% Hausdorff distance, and average symmetric surface distances (ASSD). In an extended validation cohort of 264 participants, CNN-derived regional volumes were analyzed across Parkinson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). CNN segmentation outperformed atlas-based segmentation across accuracy metrics. Overall medians were 0.75 vs 0.33 for Dice, 2.0 vs 5.0 mm for 95% Hausdorff distance, and 0.30 vs 1.02 mm for ASSD. CNN-derived volumetry recapitulated established disease-associated patterns, including predominant mesencephalic, superior cerebellar peduncle, and red nucleus atrophy in PSP and more marked pontine and middle cerebellar peduncle volume loss in MSA. The principal contribution of this study is an atrophy-robust multiclass brainstem segmentation framework. This framework may enable anatomically more faithful extraction of quantitative MRI metrics than atlas-based approaches and may reduce contamination from adjacent CSF spaces, particularly in small atrophy-affected structures.

title: Inter-subject receive-template substitution for quantitative brain water content mapping at 3 T: a leave-one-out evaluation.
abstract: To evaluate a configuration-specific inter-subject receive template as an alternative to participant-specific receive referencing within the evaluated 3 T scanner configuration. Datasets from twenty-five healthy subjects were analyzed using a strict leave-one-participant-out method. Each degree-3 template used the other 24 participants. Arm E used a participant-specific effective relative receive divisor; Arm T used the held-out template. Both arms underwent independent, identically defined residual calibration, including a local intercept (C0), its spatially regularized field (μ), and the mean-normalized form used downstream (μ). This was followed by ventricular-CSF calibration. Primary outcomes were participant-level median quantitative water content (qWC) in white and gray matter; whole brain was secondary. Paired bias, mean absolute error (MAE), Bland-Altman limits, Pearson r, and Lin concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) were calculated. Mean relative receive-template mismatch was 2.273% (standard deviation (SD), 0.568%; range, 1.431%-3.615%). Mean Arm T minus Arm E differences were -0.04 percentage units (p.u.; dimensionless water fraction relative to pure water = 100 p.u.) in white matter and -0.17 p.u. in gray matter; MAE was 0.17 and 0.22 p.u., and CCC was 0.991 and 0.989, respectively. Whole-brain bias was -0.12 p.u. (MAE, 0.19 p.u.; CCC, 0.993). Bland-Altman widths were below 1 p.u. Exploratory associations between global mismatch and qWC disagreement were weak; all 95% participant-bootstrap confidence intervals spanned zero. Under symmetric arm-specific calibration, the configuration-specific template produced qWC estimates in close agreement with the participant-specific explicit reference strategy. This internal matched-configuration result supports technical feasibility but does not establish formal equivalence, interchangeability, or external generalization.

title: Learning from deaths to improve lives: why England still needs a national LeDeR programme.
journal: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science
abstract: The National Health Service England's Learning from Lives and Deaths of People with a Learning Disability and Autistic People programme is the world's only national mortality review system for people with intellectual disability. Abandoning national mortality surveillance risks making preventable deaths less visible, with profound consequences for equity in healthcare.

title: Blind spots in Australian bipolar disorder surveillance: Limitations of population-based and consumer needs surveys.
journal: The Australian and New Zealand journal of psychiatry
abstract: Population-based surveys provide a critical means of characterising the prevalence, burden, lived experience, service use and unmet needs associated with bipolar disorder, including among people who may not be engaged with formal healthcare services. However, existing Australian survey efforts are often cross-sectional, outdated and affected by important sampling and ascertainment biases. Administrative and linked datasets can provide complementary information on service use and outcomes, but their reach is constrained by the absence of an integrated national data system and their reliance on contact with health and other services. Consequently, current surveillance approaches provide an incomplete picture of bipolar disorder in Australia. Despite its considerable burden, substantial unmet need persists in diagnosis, treatment and service provision, even though many people with bipolar disorder can achieve recovery with timely and appropriate care. In this Perspectives-Viewpoint article, we argue that more inclusive, longitudinal and co-designed national surveillance is needed to accurately characterise bipolar disorder and generate the evidence required to guide investment, service planning and reform.

title: Severe Intracranial Hemorrhage in an Infant with Mild Factor XI Deficiency: Diagnostic Role of Neuroimaging.
Autism screening outcomes in a mental health crisis population: findings from a service evaluation.
abstract: We evaluated proportions of autism screening outcomes among adults accessing crisis mental health services in Sussex, UK, and examined associations with quality of life and joint hypermobility as an indicator of physiological complexity. Fifty-five participants (mean age 35.7 years, 56% male, 85% White) completed autism and hypermobility screening questionnaires and the Mental Health Quality of Life Questionnaire. Forty-three participants (78%) scored above screening threshold for autism, although only eight had a prior diagnosis, and 27% scored above the published autistic median.
