Higher Ritvo Autism and Asperger Diagnostic Scale (RAADS-14) scores were associated with lower quality of life (p < 0.001) and poorer well-being (p < 0.01). Those screening positive for hypermobility also had higher RAADS-14 scores (p = 0.01), suggesting a possible biological contribution to distress. Findings indicate high frequency of possible autism in crisis services and a need for tailored, biopsychosocially informed support.

title: Operational definitions of the asymptomatic TTR variant carrier: a methodological framework for ATTRv amyloidosis polyneuropathy research.

title: Multifunctional Hyaluronic Acid-functionalized Liposomes for Targeted Astaxanthin Delivery in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Cells.
abstract: Astaxanthin (AST), a marine-derived carotenoid with potent antioxidant and anticancer activities, is limited in pharmaceutical application by poor aqueous solubility and low bioavailability. In this study, we developed a multifunctional liposomal delivery system integrating Hyaluronic Acid (HA)-mediated targeting, PEGylation, and phytosterol ester-based membrane stabilization for targeted AST delivery in Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) cells. HA-functionalized AST Liposomes (HA@AST-Lip) with different HA modification ratios were prepared and characterized for physicochemical properties, stability, release, and bioaccessibility. Cellular uptake was evaluated in the Huh-7 HCC cell line, with HA blocking to further investigate HA-CD44-mediated interactions. The in vitro effects on cell viability, migration, apoptosis, and related gene expression were evaluated. HA@AST-Lip exhibited favorable nanoscale characteristics, high encapsulation efficiency, and desirable storage stability. In vitro digestion studies demonstrated sustained release behaviors and significantly improved AST bioaccessibility compared with free AST. Cellular uptake analysis showed enhanced internalization of HA@AST-Lip, possibly via CD44-mediated interactions. Compared with free AST, HA@AST-Lip more effectively inhibited cell proliferation and migration and promoted apoptosis. In addition, HA@AST-Lip modulated the expression of apoptosis- and migration- related genes, which may partially involve NF-κB-related signaling. The findings suggest that HA@AST-Lip improved the bioaccessibility and cellular delivery of AST, with enhanced anticancer effects potentially associated with HA-CD44-mediated uptake and NF-κB-related signaling. However, further in vivo studies are needed to validate its therapeutic efficacy and biosafety. These findings demonstrate that HA-functionalized liposomes can improve the delivery performance and anticancer potential of AST, providing a promising lipid-based nanoplatform for HCC-targeted therapy.

title: Doxorubicin Nanocarriers in Glioblastoma Therapy: Advances and Limitations.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive brain malignancies, with limited therapeutic success largely due to the restrictive nature of the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) and intrinsic drug resistance mechanisms. Despite standard treatment strategies, the median survival remains approximately 16 months, underscoring the urgent need for more effective therapeutic approaches. Doxorubicin (DOX), a potent anthracycline chemotherapeutic, has demonstrated significant anticancer activity; however, its clinical application in GBM is severely hindered by poor BBB permeability, active efflux mediated by transporters such as P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and Breast Cancer Resistance Protein (BCRP), and dose-limiting systemic toxicity. To overcome these limitations, this review focuses on Drug Delivery Systems (DDS) for DOX-loaded polymeric, magnetic, proteinbased, liposome nanocarriers, dendrimers, and Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) for BBB-targeted GBM therapy. In particular, functionalised PLGA Nanoparticles (NPs), iron oxide NPs, Ferritin (Ft), Apoferritin (AFt), Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA), peptide-functionalised liposomes, PAMAM dendrimers, and exosomes have been studied in preclinical GBM models. Despite preclinical studies showing better brain delivery and anticancer activity, DOX-loaded nanocarriers exhibit varying potencies depending on their physicochemical properties and design strategies. Herein, drug loading, encapsulation efficiency, particle size, targeting ability, model systems, and administration route were examined. Key limitations, including biological barriers, physicochemical instability, and heterogeneity in experimental models, remain critical obstacles to achieving robust and reproducible outcomes across DOX-loaded nanocarriers.

title: The Seizure-related Homolog (SEZ6) Family in Cancer: Emerging Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets.
abstract: Cancer is a global burden, contributing to about 20 million incident cases and around 10 million mortalities in 2022. Metastasis, or secondary tumor formation, is the prevalent cause of most mortalities. Metastasis and resistance to therapy are major contributors to cancer-related mortality. Expression shifts of cytoplasmic, nuclear, cell-surface, and transmembrane proteins play an important role in tumor progression and therapeutic targeting. This review summarizes the family of SEZ6 proteins, which are single-transmembrane proteins. The family comprises Seizure-related 6 homolog (SEZ6), SEZ6-like (SEZ6L), and SEZ6-like 2 (SEZ6L2) proteins. These proteins are studied for their primary roles in synaptic connectivity, signal transduction, protein interactions, and the mediation of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. However, the SEZ6 family proteins have also been identified as emerging biomarkers and therapeutic targets across various cancers. Recent studies have shown that SEZ6L2 and SEZ6L, not SEZ6, are involved in complement regulation, which can lead to tumor escape and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. This review summarises the multifaceted roles of SEZ6 family members in modulating the complement system, their expression patterns, prognostic relevance, and the proposed molecular mechanisms underlying tumor aggressiveness, migration, and other malignant phenotypes. This study also discusses the recent advances in SEZ6-targeted ADCs, biomarker-driven patient selection, and future opportunities for cancer biology.

title: Structure-Activity Relationships and Mechanistic Insights of Racetam Derivatives in Epilepsy Management.
journal: Central nervous system agents in medicinal chemistry
abstract: Epilepsy continues to affect millions globally, and despite advances in treatment, many patients still struggle with drug-resistant forms of the disorder. Among the newer therapeutic options, racetam derivatives have garnered attention for their distinctive mechanism of action-modulating synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A)-which distinguishes them from traditional antiepileptic drugs (AEDs). This review provides a closer examination of the structure-activity relationships (SAR) of racetam analogues, investigating how chemical modifications, such as aromatic substitution, halogenation, and alkyl chain extension, can significantly enhance key properties, including lipophilicity, blood-brain barrier penetration, metabolic stability, and receptor binding. By comparing well-known agents like piracetam and levetiracetam with newer, more refined molecules such as brivaracetam and seletracetam, we highlight the steady evolution in potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetics. We also explore emerging strategies that aim to address current challenges in drug delivery and tolerability, ranging from stereochemical optimization to nanotechnology-based formulations and prodrug design. Recent findings from both preclinical and clinical studies (2021-2024) underscore the growing relevance of racetams in epilepsy care, highlighting the need for continued innovation in medicinal chemistry and translational research. Ultimately, racetam derivatives represent a compelling intersection of pharmaceutical design and neuropharmacology, offering a promising roadmap for the development of next-generation AEDs tailored to individual patient needs.

title: Elevated TMAO is Associated with Pulmonary Arterial Endothelial Cell Pyroptosis and Sumoylation-Related Caspase-1 Signaling in MCT-Induced Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Rats.
abstract: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) is characterized by progressive pulmonary vascular remodeling, in which Pulmonary Arterial Endothelial Cell (PAEC) dysfunction and inflammation play important roles. The gut microbiota-derived metabolite trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) has been associated with PAH and vascular inflammation, but the relationship between TMAO, PAEC pyroptosis, and post-translational regulation of Caspase-1 in PAH remains incompletely understood. The association between elevated TMAO and PAEC pyroptosis and SUMOylation-related Caspase-1 signaling in monocrotaline (MCT)-induced PAH was investigated. PAH was induced in rats by a single intraperitoneal injection of MCT (60 mg/kg). Hemodynamic parameters, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling were assessed. Plasma TMAO, IL-1β, and IL-18 levels were measured, whereas GSDMD, Caspase-1, and SUMO-1 expression in CD31-positive pulmonary arterial endothelial cells was examined by immunofluorescence. Potential SUMOylation sites on Caspase-1 were predicted using SUMOplot, JASSA, and GPS-SUMO. 3,3-Dimethyl- 1-butanol (DMB), a microbial TMA production inhibitor, was used to reduce circulating TMAO levels. MCT-induced PAH was accompanied by increased plasma TMAO levels, pulmonary vascular remodeling, right ventricular hypertrophy, increased GSDMD expression in CD31-positive PAECs, and elevated circulating IL-1β and IL-18. Bioinformatic analyses identified several putative SUMOylation sites on Caspase-1, with K256 showing a high prediction score. SUMO-1 and Caspase-1 expression were also increased in PAECs from MCT-treated rats. DMB treatment reduced circulating TMAO levels and attenuated hemodynamic abnormalities, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling. These changes were accompanied by reduced GSDMD, SUMO-1, and Caspase-1 expression and lower plasma IL-1β and IL-18 levels. Elevated circulating TMAO in MCT-induced PAH was accompanied by increased GSDMD, SUMO-1, and Caspase-1 expression in PAECs and elevated plasma IL-1β and IL-18 levels, whereas reduction of TMAO by DMB attenuated these molecular changes together with pulmonary vascular remodeling. These findings extend the previously recognized association between TMAO and PAH by linking elevated TMAO to pyroptosis-associated alterations in the pulmonary arterial endothelium. The coordinated changes in SUMO-1 and Caspase-1, together with the bioinformatic prediction of potential SUMOylation sites on Caspase-1, further suggest the possible involvement of SUMOylation-related Caspase-1 signaling. However, direct SUMO conjugation of Caspase-1 and modification of the predicted K256 site were not experimentally demonstrated; therefore, this regulatory mechanism remains a hypothesis requiring further validation. Elevated TMAO is associated with enhanced PAEC pyroptosis-related signaling and coordinated increases in SUMO-1 and Caspase-1 expression in MCT-induced PAH. Reducing circulating TMAO with DMB attenuates these molecular abnormalities, pulmonary hemodynamic alterations, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling. These findings support a potential link between TMAO and SUMOylation-related Caspase-1 signaling in PAH and identify this pathway as a candidate mechanism for future investigation.

title: Rivastigmine and Emerging Nanotechnological Strategies for Targeted Delivery: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease affects millions of people globally; it is an irreversible and incurable disease, characterized by gradual cognitive decline as well as pathophysiological changes including the presence of senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. There are several risk factors associated with Alzheimer's disease, including elevated blood pressure, blood sugar concentration, alcohol consumption, smoking, and sleep disturbances. Rivastigmine is an FDA-approved cholinesterase inhibitor used to treat Alzheimer's disease. It is available as oral solutions, capsules, and transdermal patches. Oral administration can lead to detrimental and off-target effects such as nausea and vomiting, and the use of patches can cause irritation and rashes. Across various systems, including the Cardiovascular (CVS), Gastrointestinal (GI), immunological, dermatological, and respiratory systems, rivastigmine has been associated with effects that further necessitate targeted drug delivery. Novel drug delivery systems such as Liposomes, Polymeric Nanoparticles, Dendrimers, Solid Lipid Nanoparticles (SLNs), Nanostructured Lipid Carriers (NLCs), nano-emulsions, and Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles (MSNs) have been developed to address the limitations of conventional dosage forms. These new formulations possess the ability to increase drug loading capacity, enhance penetration across the BBB, reduce expulsion, and offer controlled release of the drug. As a result, rivastigmine can be targeted to the intended site, with fewer off-target effects. However, formulation-specific toxicity may still occur. Positive off-target effects, such as improved appetite, protection against malnutrition, and evidence of advantage in treating colitis, were also observed with rivastigmine. However, detailed studies of its mechanism of action are needed to provide a scientifically sound justification for repurposing rivastigmine. Google Scholar and PubMed were searched for literature for this review and included studies that met the criteria.

title: Pharmacokinetics, Metabolism, Disposition, and Neuropharmacological Mechanisms of Jujuboside A: A Review.
abstract: Insomnia is a frequently occurring sleep disorder that is associated with a reduced quality of life and a higher risk of neuropsychological, metabolic, and inflammatory diseases. Jujuboside A (JuA), a dammarane-type triterpenoid saponin obtained from Ziziphi Spinosae Semen (Suanzaoren), has shown promise as a therapeutic agent for insomnia. The present review summarizes the available evidence re-garding the pharmacokinetics, metabolism, disposition, sedative-hypnotic activity, and neuroprotective effects of JuA. It is believed that JuA acts as a multi-target agent for both the treatment of insomnia and for providing neuroprotection, even though it has a low oral bioavailability (about 1.32%) and limited ability to penetrate the brain (with a brain-to-plasma ratio of 0.1-0.3). JuA is subject to extensive metab-olism in the intestine and liver, this being performed via the body's glycosidases and by the gut microbi-ota, and is eliminated via both the biliary and renal routes. The drug seems to influence sleep mainly through GABAergic signaling in the Paraventricular Thalamic Nucleus (PVT), and also impacts the monoaminergic and adenosinergic pathways, the circadian rhythm, mitochondrial function in prefrontal neurons, and gut-brain interactions. The neuroprotective effects involve various pathways including Shh/Gli1/Gli2, P2X7R-BDNF, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK/ERK, Wnt/β-catenin, and YY1-mediated tran-scriptional regulation. Although the existing evidence points to the therapeutic potential of JuA, more research is still required in order to better understand its pharmacological properties and mechanisms of action. This review aims to outline the pharmacological properties and molecular features of JuA, point out the current research gaps, and suggest possible avenues for the development of therapies based on JuA.

title: Dopaminergic System: A Potential Therapeutic Target for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases.
abstract: Dopamine is a critical neurotransmitter involved in the regulation of motor control, cognition, reward processing, motivation, and neuroendocrine functions. Increasing evidence indicates that disturbances in dopaminergic neurotransmission contribute significantly to the pathogenesis of major neurodegenerative disorders, particularly Parkinson's Disease (PD) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD). The dopaminergic system comprises specialized neuronal populations, dopamine receptors, and transporter proteins that collectively maintain synaptic dopamine homeostasis and neuronal signaling. Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons is a hallmark of PD, whereas emerging studies suggest that impaired dopamine signaling also plays an important role in the cognitive and behavioral deficits associated with AD. This review summarizes current knowledge regarding the involvement of dopaminergic pathways in neurodegeneration, with emphasis on receptor subtypes, dopamine transporter function, and neuronal vulnerability. Furthermore, it discusses established therapeutic interventions, including dopamine receptor agonists and other dopaminergic modulators, highlighting their clinical benefits and limitations. Recent advances in the field, such as biased receptor ligands, gene-based therapies, stem cell-mediated regeneration, and nanoparticle-assisted drug delivery systems, are also evaluated for their potential to enhance therapeutic efficacy and target specificity. In addition, commonly used experimental models for investigating dopaminergic dysfunction and disease progression are reviewed. Despite substantial progress, several translational challenges continue to hinder the development of disease-modifying treatments. A deeper understanding of dopaminergic signaling mechanisms and their interactions with neurodegenerative processes may facilitate the identification of novel therapeutic targets. Future strategies should focus not only on symptomatic management but also on slowing or preventing disease progression through precise modulation of dopaminergic networks.

title: Modeling the cost-effectiveness of NVX-CoV2705 and the public health impact of vaccination for the prevention of seasonal COVID-19 in the US.
abstract: Older adults and those with comorbidities have increased risk of severe disease and mortality from COVID-19. This analysis estimated the cost-effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccination versus no vaccination in the US and potential impact of increased vaccine coverage. A Markov-based model was updated using the latest epidemiology and vaccine reactogenicity data. Cases, costs, and outcomes for individuals aged 18-64 with ≥1 comorbidity and ≥65 years were estimated for NVX-CoV2705 (Nuvaxovid) versus no vaccination from a third-party payer perspective. Scenario analyses considered the societal perspective and analogous comparisons for BNT162b2 (Comirnaty), mRNA-1273 (Spikevax), and mRNA-1283 (mNEXSPIKE). Results were scaled for public health impact analyses. Base-case results associated NVX-CoV2705 with fewer cases (0.0447), hospitalizations (0.0037), and deaths (0.0004) per person on average. NVX-CoV2705 yielded an ICER of $9,840/QALY gained, reflecting fewer QALYs lost (0.0039) alongside increased direct costs ($38.09) per person. Differences for mRNA vaccines were driven by price and reactogenicity. Increasing vaccine coverage by 5-15 percentage points resulted in 114-341 hospitalizations and 11-33 deaths averted per 1,000,000 individuals. NVX-CoV2705 was predicted to be cost-effective over no vaccination. This analysis included a more granular approach to modeling reactogenicity events, an important consideration in vaccine cost-effectiveness analyses.

title: [Josef Hyrtl on the etymology of certain terms in general neuroanatomy].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: This paper presents a translation of selected sections from the monograph «Onomatologia anatomica» (1880) authored by the Austrian physician and anatomist Josef Hyrtl. The focus is on the etymology of certain terms within the domain of general neuroanatomy, specifically «Ependyma,» «Ganglion,» «Motorius/Sensitivus,» «Nervus, Nervosus, Neurula,» and «Neurilema/Neurhymen.».

title: Cryo-EM and NMR Reveal a Membrane-Gated Doc2B-Munc13-1 Complex and a Helical Doc2B-SNARE-Binding Interface.
abstract: Doc2s modulate neurotransmitter release through interactions with Munc13-1, SNAREs, lipids, and Ca2+, which involve the Doc2 C2 domains and Munc13-interacting domain (MID). However, it is unclear how these interactions are coupled, how Doc2s bind to Munc13-1, and how they bind to the SNAREs. Here we determined the cryo-electron microscopy structure of a Doc2B-Munc13-1 complex aided by an AI-designed Munc13-1 binder, revealing how Doc2B MID binds to a Munc13-1 hydrophobic pocket essential for opening syntaxin-1 and explaining why Doc2B inhibits SNARE assembly. NMR and fluorescence spectroscopy show that Doc2B MID binds lipids and that MID-lipid and MID-Munc13-1 interactions are mutually exclusive, suggesting that membrane binding helps release the inhibition of Munc13-1. NMR shows that Doc2B binds to the SNARE complex via two helices of C2B. Based on these results and liposome fusion assays, we propose a working model whereby: 1. Doc2B MID-Munc13-1 interactions facilitate synergistic binding of both proteins to the plasma membrane, with the MID inhibiting Munc13-1. 2. Membrane binding facilitates MID-lipid interactions that transiently relieve the inhibition of Munc13-1, allowing SNARE complex assembly. 3. Doc2B binding to the SNARE complex inhibits neurotransmitter release but generates a primed state that mediates neurotransmitter release by an as-yet-unknown mechanism.

title: Real-World Status of Augmentation Therapy With Atypical Antipsychotics in Major Depressive Disorder: A Claims Database Study.
abstract: This study investigated pharmacotherapy treatment patterns, focusing on atypical antipsychotics (AAP) augmentation therapy, in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) who initiated antidepressant monotherapy in Japan. This retrospective cohort study was conducted using a large Japanese claims database. Patients with MDD aged ≥ 18 years who were subsequently prescribed antidepressants between June 2013 and June 2020 were enrolled. We identified patients who initiated antidepressant monotherapy as the first line of treatment (LOT1). Treatment patterns, including the number, duration, and sequence of LOTs, were examined before and after AAP augmentation therapy. In total, 50 355 patients received antidepressant monotherapy in LOT1; the most common therapy was selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). The use of AAP augmentation therapy increased with progression of LOTs. Overall, 3811 patients (7.6%) received AAP augmentation therapy after a mean of 1.4 LOTs and 270 days from treatment initiation. Although 37.9% of these patients changed to other treatments in the next LOT within 180 days, 46.4% continued AAP augmentation therapy for ≥ 180 days. Among patients receiving antidepressant monotherapy in LOT1, 14.6% underwent ≥ 3 LOTs and the most common treatment pattern was SSRI-SSRI-SSRI. The proportion of patients receiving AAP augmentation therapy was low. Although few LOTs were required before AAP augmentation therapy, the claims-defined interval before AAP augmentation therapy was relatively long. Approximately half of the patients demonstrated prescription persistence with AAP augmentation therapy for ≥ 180 days. These findings may help clinicians refine treatment strategies regarding the timing of AAP augmentation, providing a basis for future research on how such adjustments might influence therapeutic outcomes in MDD.

title: [Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 4].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) is a heterogeneous group of hereditary disorders characterized by iron accumulation in the brain, predominantly affecting the basal ganglia. These conditions present with multisystem clinical manifestations, most notably motor, cognitive, and behavioral disorders. To date, ten variants of NBIA have been identified, with BPAN, PKAN, and PLAN being the most common. This report presents five confirmed cases of type 4 NBIA, termed mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration (MPAN), detailing clinical and neuroimaging findings and its molecular genetic characteristics; MPAN is associated with mutations in the C19orf12 gene encoding a mitochondrial membrane protein.

title: [Levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination in chronotherapy of Parkinson's disease].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of the levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination in the chronotherapy of Parkinson's disease (PD). This multicenter study was conducted at seven clinical sites, with 72 patients completing the follow-up period. The efficacy of levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone administration was evaluated in relation to the daily activity profile of levodopa. Patients recorded hourly assessments of «on», «off», and dyskinesia periods in a diary before and after therapy adjustment. The follow-up period lasted one month. Patients misidentified «on» periods in 46% of cases and «off» periods in 35% of cases. The daily profile of levodopa efficacy was heterogeneous: the favorable period occurred in the morning for 40% of patients, in the afternoon for 32%, in the evening for 21%, and in the late evening for 7%. Tailoring levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone administration to the circadian profile improved outcomes in 72% of patients. A morning peak in efficacy predicted high drug sensitivity, while shifting the favorable period to the evening was associated with lower therapy efficacy. Optimizing the timing of antiparkinsonian drug administration in accordance with the circadian rhythm of PD symptoms may enhance therapeutic efficacy. Chronotherapy that incorporates the circadian profile of levodopa efficacy can maximize the benefits of levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone combination therapy.

title: [Anhedonia in Parkinson's disease: findings from the first national clinical and statistical study of motor and non-motor associations].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: To evaluate anhedonia severity in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) and examine its associations with demographic, motor, and non-motor characteristics. The study included 390 patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. Participants were classified into two groups by anhedonia severity: without anhedonia (<3 points; 77 patients, 19.7%) and with anhedonia (≥3 points; 313 patients, 80.3%). All participants underwent comprehensive clinical and neurological evaluations. The variables analyzed included age, age at PD onset, disease duration, Hoehn and Yahr stage, rate of progression, presence of dyskinesias, Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) scores I-III, total UPDRS score, Schwab-England scale, anxiety, depression, cognitive status, sleep quality, apathy, and asthenia. Statistical analyses included the Mann-Whitney test, Spearman's correlation analysis, and multivariate linear regression with robust standard errors. The cohort's median anhedonia score was 4.0 [3.0; 6.0] points. Statistically significant correlations were identified between anhedonia and depressive symptoms (ρ=0.668; p<0.001; q<0.001), anxiety (ρ=0.277; p<0.001; q=0.001), Hoehn and Yahr stage (ρ=0.208; p<0.001; q<0.001), patient age (ρ=0.187; p<0.001; q=0.001), age at disease onset (ρ=0.145; p=0.006; q=0.025), and cognitive status (ρ=-0.199; p=0.009; q=0.028). Comparative analysis showed that patients with anhedonia had higher depression scores (9.0 [7.0; 11.0] versus 5.0 [4.0; 7.0] points; p<0.001; q<0.001), were older (68.0 [63.0; 74.0] versus 65.0 [58.0; 71.0] years; p=0.003; q=0.020), had lower cognitive status scores (23.0 [20.0; 25.0] versus 25.0 [24.0; 27.0] points; p=0.009; q=0.042), and lower sleep quality scores (12.0 [6.0; 18.0] versus 18.0 [14.8; 22.2] points; p=0.002; q=0.020). In the multivariate regression model, depressive symptoms were the only independent predictor of anhedonia severity (β=0.509; 95% CI 0.329 to 0.689; p<0.001; q<0.001). Anhedonia is a prevalent non-motor manifestation of PD, identified in most patients in this cohort. It is most strongly associated with depressive symptoms, which remain independently significant in multivariate analysis. Anhedonia is not directly related to motor severity, disease duration, dyskinesias, or functional independence. These results suggest that anhedonia is primarily an affective non-motor component of PD and should be specifically assessed in clinical practice.

title: [Evolution of strategies for selecting dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: Over the past five decades, strategies for dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease (PD) have evolved significantly. Historically treatments aimed to reduce parkinsonism symptoms. Later, the focus shifted to preventing motor fluctuations and dyskinesias, leading clinicians to delay levodopa initiation. As knowledge of the mechanisms underlying motor complications, the clinical relevance of non-motor symptoms, and the efficacy and safety profiles of various dopaminergic drug classes increased, clinicians developed a personalized approach to therapy selection. This article reviews the scientific concepts that informed current approaches to dopaminergic therapy in PD. It evaluates clinical studies comparing levodopa and dopamine receptor agonists as initial therapies, the rationale for revising the strategy of delaying levodopa initiation, and current principles for treatment selection at different disease stages. The analysis addresses patient age and age at PD onset, severity of motor and non-motor symptoms, risk factors for motor fluctuations and dyskinesias, cognitive and psychiatric status, and individual susceptibility to adverse effects from dopaminergic therapy. The article also examines the benefits and limitations of different dopaminergic drug classes. The findings suggest that current strategies prioritize personalized and rational use of dopaminergic agents at various stages of PD, tailored to the patient's clinical profile.

title: [Nosological spectrum of disorders characterized by the combination of cerebellar ataxia and parkinsonism].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: The differential diagnosis of disorders characterized by the combination of cerebellar ataxia and parkinsonism presents significant challenges. This combination is observed across a wide range of sporadic and hereditary neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic diseases, and acquired (secondary) conditions. Multisystem atrophy represents the most common disorder manifesting both ataxia and parkinsonism. Additional common conditions include fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), Wilson-Konovalov disease, and autosomal-dominant spinocerebellar ataxias types 1, 2, 3, 17, and 27B. Other nosological entities are considerably less prevalent. This review provides concise descriptions and emphasizes the most relevant differential diagnostic features of disorders presenting with cerebellar ataxia and parkinsonism.

title: [Serum markers of intestinal and blood-brain barrier permeability (zonulin and claudin-5) in patients with Parkinson's disease].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: This study aimed to assess serum concentrations of intestinal and blood-brain barrier permeability markers, specifically zonulin and claudin-5, in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) and in those with stage one and two dyscirculatory encephalopathy (DE). The study also evaluated the relationship between these marker levels and the clinical features of the diseases. This cross-sectional comparative study included 146 patients (116 with PD and 30 with DE). Serum levels of zonulin and claudin-5 peptides were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Copy number variations in the SNCA, Parkin, UCHL1, PINK1, DJ1, LRRK2, and ATP13A2 genes were analyzed by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA), while GBA1 variants were assessed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Claudin-5 levels were significantly higher in patients with PD compared to the control group: 2.5 [1.3; 3.8] ng/mL in patients with PD versus 1.0 [0.3; 2.5] ng/mL in patients with DE (p=0.001). Zonulin levels were also higher in patients with PD than in the DE group, at 48.0 [34.5; 59.8] ng/mL versus 40.1 [21.7; 55.0] ng/mL, respectively. Zonulin concentration showed a positive correlation with MMSE scores (ρ=0.20; p<0.0001) and MoCA scores (ρ=0.19; p<0.0001). Zonulin levels were inversely correlated with the score on the third part of the MDS-UPDRS scale (ρ=-0.18; p<0.0001). Claudin-5 levels were highest in patients with early-stage PD (2.6 [1.8; 4.2] ng/mL), compared with 2.3 [1.0; 3.7] ng/mL in advanced-stage PD and 1.0 [0.3; 2.5] ng/mL in patients with DE (p=0.001). Pairwise comparisons revealed a statistically significant difference between the early-stage PD subgroup and the DE group. Similarly, patients with early-stage PD had the highest median zonulin concentration (51.8 [41.3; 58.4] ng/mL), compared with 40.0 [32.0; 59.8] ng/mL in the advanced group and 40.1 [21.7; 55.0] ng/mL in patients with DE (p=0.041). In the main group, mutations in PD-associated genes were identified in 32 patients. Claudin-5 levels were higher in patients with PD than in the DE group for both genetic and sporadic forms (p=0.004). Claudin-5 levels did not differ significantly between genetic and sporadic forms of PD (p=0.824). Zonulin levels were significantly higher in patients with genetic forms of PD compared to both sporadic forms (p=0.007) and the DE group (p=0.006). Sporadic forms of PD did not differ significantly from the comparison group in zonulin levels (p=0.746). Overall, intergroup differences in zonulin were statistically significant (p=0.001). Assessing specific changes in intestinal and blood-brain barrier permeability markers in patients with PD is a significant area of research for understanding the disease's pathogenesis. Further investigation is necessary to predict disease progression and to identify potential targets for pathogenetic therapy.

title: [Molecular biomarkers for multiple system atrophy. (A systematic review)].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Early diagnosis remains challenging because of clinical heterogeneity and symptom overlap with Parkinson's disease and other atypical parkinsonian syndromes. This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on molecular biomarkers of MSA in biological fluids, including cerebrospinal fluid and blood plasma, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses). It evaluates seven groups of potential biomarkers: aggregated α-synuclein, neurofilament light chains, tau protein, myelin basic protein, neurotransmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, β-endorphins), neuroinflammation markers (cytokines, c), homocysteine, and coenzyme Q10. The review critically assesses their pathophysiological relevance, differential diagnostic and prognostic value, and the limitations and inconsistencies that hinder clinical implementation. It also discusses promising strategies for combining biomarkers.

title: [Consensus on definitions, terminology, classification of dystonia, and clinical guidelines. Part 2. Etiology and pathogenesis (Axis II). Novel genetic classification].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: This article presents an adapted Russian-language version of the 2025 International Consensus on the Classification of Dystonia, with particular emphasis on etiology and pathogenesis (Axis II). The revised classification integrates recent advances in the understanding of the biological mechanisms underlying dystonia. Axis II distinguishes between genetic and acquired etiologies, clarifies the anatomical classification of nervous system lesions, and introduces a new category for pathogenetic mechanisms, including developmental, degenerative, metabolic, and immune or inflammatory processes. The article highlights the adoption of the modern genetic nomenclature (Movement Disorder Society - MDS), which replaces the previous DYT locus system. A detailed analysis is provided for the pathogenetic mechanisms of drug-induced, autoimmune, and neurodegenerative forms of dystonia. The final section outlines etiopathogenetic therapies, including incobotulinum toxin A and neurosurgical interventions. The proposed two-axis system aims to systematize clinical data and improve the accuracy of dystonia diagnosis for both specialists and physicians in related fields.

title: [Consensus on definitions, terminology, classification of dystonia, and clinical guidelines. Part 1. Historical context, definitions, terminology, and clinical characteristics (Axis i)].
journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova
abstract: This study analyzes current international approaches to the definition, terminology, classification, and clinical phenomenology of dystonia, adapts the 2025 international consensus for Russian clinical practice, and develops a unified Russian-language terminological standard. A panel of ten Russian movement disorder experts developed the consensus. The analysis included the 2013 and 2025 international consensus statements, clinical guidelines, and publications on the classification, phenomenology, pathophysiology, genetics, and treatment of dystonia indexed in PubMed and Web of Science (2013-2026). Terminology, definitions, and practical recommendations were established through expert discussions. An adapted Russian-language version of the 2025 international consensus on Axis I of the clinical classification of dystonia is presented. The current disease definition, terminological standards, clinical phenomena, and accompanying signs of dystonia have been clarified. Terms not recommended for use have been identified, and algorithms for clinical assessment and differential diagnosis are proposed. Contemporary approaches to symptomatic therapy are outlined, with botulinum toxin type A recommended as first-line therapy for most focal and segmental forms of dystonia. This consensus unifies terminology and clinical assessment of dystonia, adapts international guidelines for Russian-speaking practice, and supports standardized diagnosis, phenomenological description, and rational therapy selection.

title: No Memory Is an Island: How Social Interactions Transform Autobiographical Memory.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
abstract: Autobiographical memory is not merely a record of past events but a dynamic reconstruction shaped by context, emotion, and social interaction. In this hypothesis paper, we propose that empathic interactions can transform autobiographical memory, altering memory's content, emotional tone, and integration into the self. We begin by outlining the social foundations of autobiographical memory and the neural systems involved in its transformation, focusing on the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala. We then explore how empathic exchanges may lead to changes in memory specificity and coherence, emotional reappraisal, and self-concept, particularly within psychotherapy and close relationships. Central to our framework is the proposal that interbrain synchrony, neural coupling across individuals during interaction, facilitates the co-construction of meaning and shared understanding. Crucially, we argue that distinct forms of empathic interaction and patterns of interbrain synchrony support different mechanisms of memory change, including contextual binding, emotional regulation, narrative reframing, and self-relevant integration. We discuss how these mechanisms support memory updating through repeated interpersonal engagement. Finally, we offer testable predictions of our model and consider clinical and societal implications. Our framework bridges memory research and social neuroscience and offers a novel, integrative direction for understanding memory as a phenomenon co-constructed through interactions.

title: Microglia: Metabolic Adaptation in Neurodegeneration.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
abstract: Microglia, the brain's primary innate immune cells, are metabolically dynamic cells whose functional states, from homeostatic surveillance to disease-associated phagocytosis, lipid droplet accumulation, and stress-induced neurotoxicity, are governed by distinct metabolic programs. Neurodegenerative stressors, including misfolded protein accumulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and sustained inflammation, initially trigger adaptive metabolic reprogramming of glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and amino acid and lipid pathways. Under chronic stimuli, these same shifts become maladaptive, impairing microglial phagocytosis, promoting lipid accumulation, and driving the secretion of neurotoxic lipid species. A unifying theme emerging across metabolic pathways is that the intermediates produced under stress, lactate, succinate, ceramide, acetyl-CoA, and α-ketoglutarate, do not merely reflect cellular state but actively reshape it through epigenetic modification of histones and DNA. In this review, we examine how each major metabolic pathway responds to acute and chronic neurodegeneration-associated stress in microglia, highlight where epigenetic mechanisms convert transient metabolic shifts into durable changes in microglial identity, and identify genetic risk factors that encode metabolic vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

title: The role of neurogenic inflammation and CGRP in migraine headache.
abstract: The last 40 years have witnessed a thorough change in our understanding of the mechanisms underlying migraine, initiated by the discovery of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). A century ago, William Bayliss, Thomas Lewis and other pioneers introduced a visionary neurophysiological mechanism, brought about by peripheral terminals of a specialized subset of primary sensory neurons, which was named 'neurogenic inflammation'; in both mammal and human skin, action potentials generated by injured nerve terminals of primary sensory neurons can invade collateral fibres via antidromic conduction and release a mediator that 'produces the flare and enhances sensitivity of other sensory axons responsible for pain'. This mediator, much later identified as CGRP, provides the missing link between these early observations and modern therapeutic targets. Multiple monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor along with orally available small molecule antagonists of the CGRP receptor have revolutionized the prevention and acute treatment of migraine. The pharmacokinetic features of anti-CGRP drugs and the paracrine actions of CGRP suggest the proposal that the mechanism underlying migraine headache occurs in a spatially limited microenvironment located outside the blood-brain barrier. According to this hypothesis, the migraine headache milieu comprises CGRP-containing peripheral sensory nerve endings (C-fibre nociceptors) and neighbouring cells, including other nerve fibres (Aδ-fibres), vascular smooth muscle cells and Schwann cells wrapping these nerve fibres.

title: The Experiences of Psychotherapy for People With Dementia: A Qualitative Interview Study With Family Members.
abstract: Psychotherapeutic interventions can support people with dementia. Family members often play a pivotal role in the therapeutic process but little is known about their experiences of therapy, how they perceive the impact on their relative, and how the experience affects them directly. This study aimed to explore the experiences of family members who engage in therapy, or support someone living with dementia to attend therapy. Individuals with dementia and their family members were recruited as participants through NHS Trusts, professional networks, social media and community and support groups based in England and Wales. Semi-structured qualitative individual or dyadic interviews were conducted with 17 participants, eight of whom were living with dementia and nine were family members. Framework analysis was used. Family members highlighted "the importance of feeling seen" as distinct individuals by clinicians when engaging with psychotherapy, and not just the carer of their partner. When working with "dementia as dynamic phenomenon", therapeutic approaches needed to balance being sufficiently structured and containing whilst allowing for adaptions to each individual changeable presentation. Participants highlighted how psychotherapy presented "expected and unexpected outcomes", challenges that arose when outcomes were not agreed upon, and how therapy functioned as a support structure in ways the participants did not foresee. Psychotherapeutic intervention provides meaningful support to the family members of individuals with dementia. Understanding the needs of family members, alongside the needs of the individual with dementia, and taking a systemic approach is conducive to better therapeutic outcomes. The changeable nature of dementia presentation means that a therapeutic approach should be flexible based on the needs of the family. Psychotherapeutic intervention with individuals with dementia can have a range of benefits for the individual and the wider family, when sufficient considerations are made to understand each person's needs.

title: Beyond Self-Report: Adding Wearable Physiological Data to Predict Dietary Restriction in Anorexia Nervosa.
journal: The International journal of eating disorders
abstract: Restricting food intake during meals is the core behavioral mechanism maintaining anorexia nervosa (AN) yet predicting when restriction occurs in daily life remains largely unexplored. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) captures negative affect preceding restriction but relies on intermittent self-report, whereas wearables can passively measure physiological signals (EPA). We investigated whether combining EMA and EPA improves prediction of restriction beyond EMA alone, hypothesizing that EMA + EPA models would outperform EMA-only models, which would outperform EPA-only models. Individuals with AN (n = 78) completed a 2-week EMA protocol while wearing an Empatica watch, completing 7151 surveys and reporting 4005 meals. Features derived from heart rate, electrodermal activity, and skin temperature were extracted across the hour before each meal. As preregistered, machine learning models were developed to predict both the occurrence and severity of self-reported restriction (logistic/linear regression, random forest, support vector machines) using EMA predictors, EPA predictors, or their combination. Contrary to our hypothesis, adding EPA predictors did not consistently improve performance. Combined models outperformed EMA-only models for some classifiers but not for logistic regression and provided no benefit for predicting severity. Models containing EMA predictors consistently outperformed EPA-only models. The best classification model was EMA-only logistic regression (AUC = 0.734), while the best regression model was EMA-only linear regression (RMSE = 1.894). Self-reported negative affect provided more information for predicting restriction than the physiological signals examined in this study. These findings suggest that self-report currently offers greater utility than wearable-derived stress physiology for identifying affect-related risk for restriction.

title: Cortical Adaptation to Muscle Fatigue Does Not Alter Early Proprioceptive Processing in Primary Sensorimotor Cortex.
abstract: Muscle fatigue potentially interferes with proprioceptive afference from peripheral "movement sensors"-the proprioceptors, which may hinder crucial sensorimotor integration and thus movement performance. However, little is known about how muscle fatigue affects cortical processing of proprioceptive afference. Twenty-four healthy volunteers (30.7 ± 6.5 years) participated in the experiment, which included magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings during 2-Hz passive ankle-joint rotations, and fatigue tasks comprised of isometric ankle plantarflexion. Corticokinematic coherence (CKC) between linear foot acceleration and MEG signals was examined before (PRE) and ~3 min after (POST) the fatigue tasks to compare the cortical proprioceptive processing. CKC peaked in the gradiometer pairs above the foot region of the primary sensorimotor (SM1) cortex in each participant. CKC strength did not show significant difference between PRE and POST at 2 Hz (0.30 ± 0.12 vs. 0.30 ± 0.14, p = 0.981) or its first harmonic at 4 Hz (0.38 ± 0.14 vs. 0.37 ± 0.13, p = 0.724). However, 4-Hz MEG power was ~30% lower in POST than in PRE. Surprisingly, fatigue-induced increase of alpha and beta power was observed bilaterally in SM1 hand regions during the ankle movements. Our results indicate that the early processing of proprioceptive afference from the ankle joint was negligibly affected by muscle fatigue or the effect recovered rapidly. The fatigue elevated alpha and beta power while diminishing neuronal activity at the 4-Hz harmonic frequency, which may reflect a compensatory mechanism for asynchronous proprioceptive afference by enhancing cortical inhibitory control.

title: Reply: Clarifying incremental accuracy and thresholds for a plasma tau-to-amyloid ratio.
Breathing may be primarily driven by the unceasing rotation of residual gravitational ischemia in the brain-'skull-trapped' regions of reduced oxygen tension.
abstract: The 'top half' of the brain sits on the 'bottom half' of the brain as a weight burden. Within the somewhat spherically shaped cranial vault, gravitational compression of the 'bottom half' of the brain against the inside of the skull, in theory, may generate ischemia, with underlying brain regions experiencing decreased blood flow and decreased oxygen tension. Some questions remain as to whether gravity is involved in the causation of breathing in humans. Is 'gravitational ischemia in the brain' a principle driver of breathing, underlying even the well-studied brainstem neuro-synchronization and automaticity mechanisms of breathing? Relevant reports from the general scientific literature were identified. A focused topical analysis of their intertwined concepts, together with their cumulative aggregate data, was done to explore the current status of this topic, as well as some possible directions for future research. One potentially testable hypothesis suggests that gravity may be a principle underlying driver for breathing, in humans, possibly working through glial cells (astrocytes), scattered throughout the brain, continuously sensing gravitationally-induced regional hypoxia in different regions of the brain, at different times, generated during different head positions, never completely resolved, and leading to a continuous repetitive triggering of the already well-established breathing automaticity mechanisms. Its position within the existing breathing neuro-circuit cascade would be at the very beginning. A second hypothesis explores the inverse of 'gravitational ischemia' in the brain, occurring in astronauts during long-duration spaceflight, and called 'gravity-opposition physiology'. This second hypothesis may potentially provide a framework for understanding Spaceflight Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome.

title: Optogenetic Stimulation of Insular Parvalbumin-Positive Interneurons Reveals CA3 Resonant Properties and Rebound Seizure Susceptibility.
abstract: Seizures in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) can spread to the insular cortex (IC) due to its connections with hippocampal and para-hippocampal areas. The contribution of specific cell types in the IC to ictogenesis remains however unclear. Therefore, we analyzed in the pilocarpine model of MTLE the effects of optogenetic activation of IC parvalbumin (PV)-positive interneurons on CA3 field activity. Light pulses were delivered at 0.5 Hz (300 s ON, 600 s OFF) in IC, between day 4 and 14 after status epilepticus in PV-ChR2 mice. During interictal periods, this procedure evoked CA3 field responses characterized by 5 Hz oscillations, which likely mirrored heightened inhibitory activity as suggested by a shift toward higher theta/beta ratio and a more negative spectral exponent. Analysis of ictal activity revealed that seizures occurred at higher rates during days of stimulation (day 4-14) compared to days with no stimulation (day 15-24) (p < 0.05). During the 300 s optogenetic stimulation cycle, seizures occurred at high rates between 301 and 502 s after the end of stimulation (p < 0.05). Our findings suggest that during the interictal phase, the synchronized activation of PV-positive interneurons in the IC imposes a GABAergic drive that, through post-inhibitory rebound mechanisms, entrains the CA3 network into a 5 Hz resonant oscillation. During states of pathological hyperexcitability, this synchronized rebound activity reaches a threshold that converts a rhythmic oscillation into a seizure. Stimulation of the IC could bias the hippocampal network toward 5 Hz oscillatory states and promote ictogenesis via inhibitory-rebound synchronization.

title: Small-Pore Chitosan Microcarriers Support Surface-Adherent Growth of Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Neural Stem Cells and Improve Intranasal Therapy of Murine Anosmia.
abstract: Intranasal delivery of neural stem cells offers a non-invasive strategy for central nervous system repair, yet its efficacy is limited by rapid mucociliary clearance and poor cellular retention. Although chitosan-based carriers have been explored, the architectural principles governing neural stem cell behavior in the intranasal microenvironment remain poorly defined. We compared chitosan microcarriers (CSMs) with three pore architectures (mean surface pore sizes 4.7 ± 1.7, 15.9 ± 3.2, and 20.5 ± 0.7 µm), fabricated via freezing-controlled phase separation, using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural stem cells (iPSC-NSCs). Cellular responses did not vary linearly with pore size: the smallest-pore formulation, CSM-196, supported surface-adhesion-dominant growth, whereas both larger-pore formulations supported infiltration-dominant growth. CSM-196 was also associated with increased proliferative activity, spontaneous neuronal differentiation, and elevated neurotrophic factor secretion without exogenous induction factors. In a methimazole-induced anosmia model, the CSM-196-iPSC-NSC formulation produced greater improvements in olfactory behavioral recovery, olfactory epithelial thickness, neuronal marker expression, and epithelial proliferation than cell-only delivery administered by the same route and schedule. This chitosan-based platform provides a surface-adhesion-oriented cell-delivery strategy that warrants further evaluation for intranasal neural regenerative therapy.

title: [Progress in research on olfactory dysfunction in patients with obstructive sleep apnea].
journal: Lin chuang er bi yan hou tou jing wai ke za zhi = Journal of clinical otorhinolaryngology head and neck surgery
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea （OSA） is a common sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by recurrent upper-airway collapse and intermittent hypoxia, which has been widely recognized for its detrimental effects on neurocognitive function and multiple physiological systems. Emerging evidence indicates that olfactory dysfunction （OD） may represent an important yet long-overlooked manifestation in patients with OSA. Numerous clinical studies have demonstrated that olfactory threshold, discrimination, and identification abilities are significantly impaired in individuals with OSA compared with healthy controls, and the severity of olfactory deficits shows a clear negative correlation with the apnea-hypopnea index. The underlying mechanisms appear to be multifactorial:①damage to the cholinergic neurotransmitter system and cognitive impairment induced by intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation;②structural and functional alterations in brain regions involved in olfactory processing, including the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus;③the impact of elevated body mass index and chronic inflammatory responses on the olfactory epithelium and central olfactory pathways. Continuous positive airway pressure （CPAP）, the first-line therapy for OSA, may partially improve olfactory performance by enhancing ventilation, reducing hypoxemia, and alleviating airway inflammation, although current evidence remains limited by sample size and follow-up duration. Beyond standard OSA management, olfactory training, neurophysiological assessment, and inflammation-modulating interventions may serve as promising future strategies. In summary, OD is highly prevalent and clinically significant in OSA patients, with a complex pathophysiological basis involving multiple interacting factors. Larger-sample, mechanism-driven, and intervention-focused studies are warranted to deepen our understanding of OSA-related OD and to support the development of more precise therapeutic approaches.

title: Catatonic signs during delirium in leptomeningeal melanoma: Treatment trade-offs in end-of-life care.
abstract: Catatonic and delirious signs overlap, creating treatment dilemmas when sedation obscures diagnostic assessment. We describe serial assessment and medication decision-making in advanced leptomeningeal melanoma during transition to home hospice. Inpatient observations, investigations, medication exposures, goals-of-care discussions, and serial Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) examinations were synthesized. A man in his late 30s with metastatic melanoma involving the leptomeninges and brain developed fluctuating arousal, inattention, disorientation, mutism, immobility, staring, withdrawal, and waxy flexibility. His Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) score decreased from 7 to 1 after intravenous lorazepam, although reassessment was limited by sedation and fluctuating wakefulness. Transient improvements in movement and speech did not translate into sustained gains in attention, communication, intake, mobility, or function. Lorazepam was subsequently reduced and discontinued when severe agitation emerged. As catatonic signs became less sustained and agitation threatened safety, scheduled haloperidol was introduced, with improvement in evening agitation and no documented extrapyramidal symptoms, oversedation, or QTc prolongation. A supervised oral-medication trial supported discharge planning, although hospice placement remained delayed by insurance barriers. A lower BFCRS score after lorazepam does not necessarily indicate meaningful clinical response if arousal, attention, and function remain impaired. In advanced cancer, catatonic signs may occur within a broader delirious or toxic-neurologic encephalopathy. Serial assessment should therefore incorporate wakefulness, attention, mobility, communication, and patient- and caregiver-defined goals. Treatment should be guided by the immediate priorities of interaction, safety, or comfort and continually reassessed in light of prognosis and feasibility of home care.

title: Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review.
abstract: Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi-element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision-making; and practical conduct of the technique.

title: No Additional Benefit of 185 Hz Versus 130 Hz at Equivalent Energy in Deep Brain Stimulation for Tremor: A Randomized Prospective Clinical Trial.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the ventral intermediate nucleus and posterior subthalamic area (VIM/PSA) in Essential Tremor (ET) and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in Parkinson's disease (PD) are established treatments for tremor. To achieve maximum tremor control, increasing stimulation frequency beyond 130 Hz is part of clinical practice, but lacks scientific evidence. To compare tremor suppression under total electrical energy delivered (TEED)-equivalent stimulation at 130 versus 185 Hz in VIM/PSA-DBS for ET and STN-DBS for PD. In this prospective, double-blind study, acute DBS effects were assessed in 18 people with ET (n = 29 hemispheres), and 25 people with PD (n = 30 hemispheres). Tremor-suppressive effects, evaluated by accelerometry, were compared with TEED-equivalent stimulation at 130 and 185 Hz using linear mixed-effects models, explorative pairwise comparisons, and equivalency testing. Linear mixed-effects models revealed no significant effect of stimulation frequency on tremor improvement in both cohorts. Pairwise comparisons showed no consistent differences in total tremor improvement with TEED-equivalent 130 Hz vs 185 Hz DBS. Post-hoc equivalence testing confirmed equivalence of stimulation frequencies under TEED-equivalent conditions within a ±20% margin of relative tremor improvement. This study provides Level II evidence that a higher stimulation frequency of 185 Hz does not offer additional benefit in deep brain stimulation for tremor in VIM/PSA for Essential Tremor or in the STN for Parkinson's Disease in the acute setting and supports 130 Hz as the standard stimulation frequency for tremor suppression.

title: Fear generalization, cross-sensitization and behavioural responses to multiple dangers in a freshwater snail.
abstract: Behavioural responses to multiple stressors play a major role in survival and fitness. In this context, an important issue that has rarely been tested is fear generalization, where responses to disparate threats are correlated at the individual level. Furthermore, while sensitization to stressors is well studied, cross-sensitization, where exposure to one threat increases behavioural responsiveness to unrelated threats, is under-studied. We exposed juvenile Physid snails (Physa acuta) to one of two disparate threats throughout their developmental period: predator cues and ash, a wildfire-derived environmental stressor. We then assayed snails' responses, relative to control snails that had no experience with either threat, to three acute exposures of each stressor. We documented consistent individual differences in snails' avoidance of predation cues and of ash. Exposure to either stressor led to sensitization at short- and long-term timescales. Importantly, snails exhibited fear generalization; individuals that avoided predation cues more strongly also avoided ash more strongly. We also documented cross-sensitization; snails reared with ash showed heightened responses to predator cues while snails reared with predator cues showed heightened responses to ash. To our knowledge, this is the first study documenting behavioural cross-sensitization for threats as disparate as predation risk and fire residue in a non-human animal.

title: Optix Regulates Abdominal Melanin Pigmentation in the Tobacco Hawkmoth Manduca sexta.
abstract: Research on butterflies has uncovered a conserved "toolkit" of genes for color pattern development and evolution. One of these genes is optix, a homeobox transcription factor that regulates ommochrome and melanin pigmentation, as well as structural coloration, in nymphalid butterflies. It remains unclear, however, whether optix plays any roles in color patterning outside of the Nymphalidae. We used CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt optix in the tobacco hornwormmoth Manduca sexta and observed a dramatic abdominal pigmentation phenotype, where orange pigmentation was replaced by black eumelanin. Chemical assays suggest that the orange pigment is not an ommochrome, indicating that optix modulates an alternative, uncharacterized pigment pathway in M. sexta. RNA-seq and chemical analyses of orange and black abdominal scales lead us to speculate that the orange pigment may be a type of melanin, perhaps N-β-alanyldopamine (NBAD) sclerotin. Our results suggest that optix plays a deeply ancestral role in pigment regulation in Lepidoptera, and demonstrates evolutionary flexibility in how it interfaces with pigment chemistry across moths and butterflies.

title: Psychobiotics for nurturing the mental health through gut-brain-signalling: current status and future directions.
abstract: The gut-microbiota-brain axis is a pivotal regulator of mental and neurological health, positioning psychobiotics as promising adjunct therapies. Specific microbial strains with inherent psychobiotic potential are known to enhance mental health, cognitive, or stress-preventive qualities. They mediate the promotion of a healthy intestinal barrier by the production of neurotransmitters, neuro-hormones and neuro-protectors, which include short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), serotonin, etc. This review explores the myriad ways that psychobiotics impact neurocognitive health and the potential use as an adjunct therapy for mental well-being. We further emphasise the revolutionary potential of nanotechnology in overcoming traditional delivery obstacles of psychobiotics with enhanced stability, bioavailability and efficacy, which are least explored in previous reviews. Hence, a detailed understanding of the development and applications of psychobiotics may offer new therapeutic possibilities and improved emotional balance. Together, these insights underscore the evolving landscape of psychobiotic research and outline future directions for developing more effective, microbiota-based interventions for mental health. The review affirms that, alongside the mechanistic effects of psychobiotics on neurocognitive health, the reinforcement of the gut-brain axis is pivotal. Thus, this review opens the scope for future investigations into personalised psychobiotics with site-directed enhanced action using nanotechnology.

title: The Association of MRI-Derived Tissue Bridge Morphometrics with Baseline Impairment and Recovery in Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury: A Subanalysis of the RISCIS Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Early prognostic biomarkers are essential to optimize treatment and trial design in spinal cord injury (SCI). The Riluzole in SCI Study (RISCIS), a multicenter randomized controlled trial, provided evidence on secondary analyses that riluzole improved functional recovery in acute cervical SCI. The current analysis uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to assess lesion and tissue bridge morphometrics against baseline impairment, functional recovery, and treatment response in RISCIS participants. In this preplanned ambispective subanalysis, 24 participants underwent T2-weighted MRI for acute cervical SCI together with neurological and functional assessments to 12 months. A subset also had diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), used to extract fractional anisotropy (FA) values. Segmentation with the Spinal Cord Toolbox (v7.2) gave ventral, dorsal, and total tissue-bridge widths and lesion volume and length. Associations with American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS) grade, upper extremity motor score (UEMS) and total motor score (TMS), lower extremity motor score (LEMS), light touch and pinprick sensory scores, Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM), and Short Form-36 (SF-36) domains at baseline and follow-up were analyzed with regression models adjusted for age and sex. Overall recovery across TMS, SCIM, and SF-36 Physical Component Summary was analyzed with an O'Brien-style global statistical test (GST). Interactions tested whether bridge metrics modified riluzole's effect. At baseline, greater ventral (β = 9.65, p = 0.017) and total (β = 6.16, p = 0.021) tissue-bridge widths were associated with higher TMS, and ventral width with higher UEMS (β = 6.61, p = 0.010). Larger dorsal (odds ratio [OR] = 21.92, p = 0.013), ventral (OR = 4.91, p = 0.049), and total (OR = 3.70, p = 0.019) bridges corresponded to less severe baseline AIS grade. Pinprick scores increased with ventral (β = 26.56, p = 0.020) and total (β = 17.50, p = 0.023) bridge width, and light touch scores increased with total bridge width (β = 16.22, p = 0.045). No imaging metric was associated with LEMS. These individual-metric associations were nominally significant but did not survive correction. In GST analyses, larger ventral (T = 4.63, p = 0.012, p'= 0.048) and total (T = 4.30, p = 0.019, p'=0.048) bridges predicted greater overall recovery; both remained significant after correction and were stable across sensitivity analyses. Ventral and total bridge width showed nominally significant interactions with riluzole treatment for upper-limb motor recovery. Exploratory DTI findings were inconclusive and sensitive to individual observations: both the FA-recovery association and the observation of poor outcome despite a preserved tissue bridge rested on a single participant. Overall, we found that midsagittal tissue-bridge width measured ∼72 h after injury from standard-of-care T2-weighted MRI was associated with baseline injury severity and multidomain functional recovery, at a timepoint substantially earlier than the 1 month at which tissue bridges have previously been quantified. Because edema may obscure lesion margins this early, acute bridge widths may underestimate spared tissue resolvable later. The treatment-interaction observation is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective confirmation. These findings support MRI-derived tissue bridges as candidate biomarkers for prognostication and enrichment of neuroprotective trials in SCI.

title: Attitudes toward eating disorders among primary care physicians.
journal: Scandinavian journal of primary health care
abstract: Eating disorders are severe conditions associated with high morbidity, mortality and socioeconomic burden. Primary care physicians are central in their early detection and treatment, but clinicians have been found to have limited knowledge and even negative attitudes toward eating disorder patients. Most studies have focused on anorexia nervosa (AN) and bulimia nervosa (BN), while less is known about attitudes toward binge eating disorder (BED) and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID). To examine primary care physicians' attitudes toward eating disorders and assess whether education and clinical experience predict comfort in management and willingness to work with affected patients. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among primary care physicians (n = 191) attending a mandatory seminar. Attitudes toward AN, BN, BED and ARFID were assessed using Likert-type items based on prior research. Ordinal logistic regression analyses examined associations between education, experience and selected attitudes. Overall attitudes were similar across diagnoses. Only 14-21% reported enjoying working with eating disorder patients. Education was consistently associated with greater comfort in management and enjoyment of working with these patients, whereas clinical experience was more strongly associated with comfort in management than with enjoyment. Familiarity with ARFID was low, reflected in reduced response rate (14.6%). Attitudes toward eating disorders were broadly similar across diagnoses, but positive attitudes toward working with affected patients were uncommon. Education was consistently associated with more favorable attitudes and greater confidence in management, highlighting the potential value of continuing professional education and support for eating disorder care in primary care.

title: NaB-induced inhibition of HDAC4 and TUG1: a novel strategy for reversing oxaliplatin resistance in colorectal cancer.
abstract: Oxaliplatin (OXA) resistance affects the efficacy of colorectal cancer (CRC) treatment. Gene expression profiles of OXA-resistant and OXA-sensitive cells were compared to identify differentially expressed non-coding RNAs. A dual-luciferase assay was used to research the targeting relationship and binding region of TUG1 and miR-449a. SiRNA interference was used to construct cell models of OXA-resistant cells with low expression of TUG1 and OXA-sensitive cells with high expression of HDAC, as well as animal models based on these two types of cells. Then, cellular function was assessed. Histopathologic conditions were assessed by immunohistochemistry. TUG1, miR-449a and Histone Deacetylase 4 (HDAC4) were all upregulated in OXA-resistant cells, and the increase of HDAC4 was accompanied by a decrease in acetylation level. TUG1 binds to miR-449a, and TUG1 was located in the cytoplasm of OXA-resistant cells. Downregulated expression of TUG1 could inhibit proliferation and induce apoptosis in OXA-resistant cells and reverse OXA resistance. Downregulated expression of HDAC4 could reduce the expression of TUG1, and inhibit proliferation and induce apoptosis of OXA-resistant cells. Treatment with 2 mmol/L sodium butyrate (NaB), a histone deacetylase inhibitor, markedly suppressed tumor cell growth through regulation of TUG1 compared with 0.01 mmol/L NaB. The OXA-resistant tumor-bearing mouse experiment further confirmed the inhibitory effect of NaB on tumor. High-dose NaB can inhibit the expression of HDAC4, and then reduce the expression of TUG1 through acetylation modification, thereby inhibiting the development of CRC and reversing OXA resistance in CRC.

title: Early sleep and sensory over-responsivity relate to insular functional connectivity with sensorimotor cortices and cerebellum in infants at varying likelihood for autism.
abstract: Sleep problems and sensory over-responsivity (SOR) are common, co-occurring, and early emerging features of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Yet, the early neural mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain unclear. Here, we used resting-state fMRI data from the Infant Brain Imaging Study (IBIS) to examine how functional brain connectivity at 6 months may relate to parent-reported measures of sleep-onset problems and SOR in infants at varying familial likelihood for ASD. The right anterior insula (rAI) - a key hub of the salience network - was used in ROI-ROI analyses to investigate functional connectivity to cortical and cerebellar regions previously implicated in sleep disruption, sensory processing challenges, and ASD. Infants at high (HL) and low (LL) likelihood for ASD displayed divergent patterns of rAI connectivity with sensorimotor cortex, as well as cerebellar regions involved in sensorimotor processing and higher-order functions. Furthermore, stronger rAI connectivity with sensorimotor cortices and cerebellar regions was associated with worse sleep-onset problems and SOR in HL infants. In contrast, stronger rAI-cerebellar connectivity was related to fewer sleep-onset problems and SOR in LL infants. Our findings indicate that altered rAI connectivity may result in over-attribution of attention to sensory stimuli and highlight aberrant sensory prediction learning, which may underlie worse sleep problems and higher SOR in HL infants.

title: Negative Affective States Are Not Detected in Rats Following an Intravenous Self-Administration Regimen Leading to Incubation of Oxycodone Craving.
abstract: In rats, cue-induced opioid craving intensifies (incubates) during abstinence from opioid self-administration and then remains high for a prolonged period. The prolonged plateau models persistent vulnerability to cue-induced craving and relapse in humans recovering from opioid use disorder. However, a very significant contributor to relapse vulnerability in these individuals is the presence of negative affective states that can persist for months to years, far beyond physical dependence. The goal of this study was to determine, for oxycodone, if the incubation of craving model recapitulates this aspect of relapse vulnerability. We began by comparing rats trained to self-administer oxycodone using a regimen leading to persistent elevation of cue-induced craving (6 h/day × 10 days) and rats trained to self-administer saline. We assessed somatic withdrawal signs in early abstinence and conducted behavioural tests modelling negative affect (open field, social preference, sucrose preference and elevated plus maze) in late abstinence. Some oxycodone rats exhibited somatic withdrawal signs on abstinence day (AD)1. However, on AD41-46, no group differences were found in behavioural tests modelling negative affect. To compare early and late abstinence periods, a second cohort of rats self-administered saline or oxycodone and then received a sequence of tests (cue-induced seeking test followed by negative affect tests) in early abstinence (AD1-7) and again in late abstinence (AD40-46). While some time-dependent changes in affect were observed within each group, they did not indicate emergence of negative affect in oxycodone rats during incubation of craving. In conclusion, our results suggest that rats exhibiting incubation are not seeking the drug to relieve an aversive state that persists into protracted abstinence. An alternative explanation is that incubated seeking reflects increased incentive salience of the drug-paired cue. Our finding of modest somatic withdrawal signs in early abstinence and no detectable negative affective states in late abstinence probably reflects lower drug intake during the intravenous regimen compared to non-contingent escalating dose regimens typically used to study withdrawal signs. Thus, while the incubation model has utility for studying cue-induced oxycodone craving, our standard incubation regimen is not suited to studying oxycodone seeking driven by the desire to relieve an aversive state.

title: Insights for the substance use disorder care continuum: findings from a qualitative study with sexual and gender minority individuals who use methamphetamine.
abstract: Methamphetamine use continues to disproportionately affect sexual and gender minority (SGM) communities and is associated with physical, mental, and sexual health harms, including heightened HIV vulnerability. While prior epidemic waves have been well documented, the current resurgence (particularly among SGM individuals), remains underexplored and occurs within an evolving HIV prevention landscape. Persistent challenges within the substance use disorder care continuum (SUDCC), including stigma and limited treatment responsiveness, underscore the need for patient-centered clinical guidance. This study examines treatment navigation experiences of SGM individuals who use methamphetamine and their recommendations for improving their substance use care. Participants were recruited from a U.S. national HIV prevention cohort that oversampled for individuals reporting recent methamphetamine use. Twenty-nine participants completed semi-structured, in-depth interviews between December 2024 and January 2025. Interviews focused on healthcare experiences, treatment navigation, and participants' recommendations for SUDCC stakeholders. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim into written transcripts, which were analyzed using a codebook approach to thematic analysis. Our findings were organized into four major themes: (1) Variation in Motivation to Use Meth, (2) Need for Destigmatized Care, (3) Desire for SGM-Affirming Care, and (4) A Spectrum of Care Needs. Participants reported a variety of motivations for using meth, including to enhance their sex lives, cognition, and emotion regulation-motivations that providers may benefit from understanding as they aim to address the overlapping physical and psychosocial health needs of patients who use methamphetamine. The importance of reducing stigma in clinical encounters was underscored frequently by participants, and represented a salient theme throughout interviews and across thematic categories. Participants described both experienced and anticipated stigma when underscoring the need for de-stigmatized substance use care, and illustrated how stigma hindered substance use care engagement and use of emergency services. Moreover, many reported a desire for community among other SGM individuals, particularly within group recovery contexts, but also elucidated the risks that accompanied drug network expansion within these treatment environments. This study advances the substance use and treatment literature by amplifying the voices of SGM individuals who use methamphetamine and providing guidance for providers who work directly with these populations.
